table.basis: Per wetland area (floodplain land or tower footprint), annual, dry phase included. Site values (g CH4 m-2 yr-1): Pantanal flooded forest BR-Npw EC 25.3 (Dalmagro 2019; the same tower is 25.6 in Delwiche 2021). Okavango seasonal floodplain BW-Nxr EC 36.3 in 2018 and 8.7 in the 2019 drought (Helfter 2021); Delwiche 2021 processes the same 2018 data to 63.1. Nxaraga chamber mean extrapolated to a full year ~22.7 (Gondwe 2021; not a measured annual). Negro interfluvial wetlands that dry for several months: Itu 10.4 and Araca 10.7 (Belger data via Ringeval 2014; Araca is diffusive only). Llanos de Moxos 51.4 per 70,000 km2 region (Amaral 2026, derived from France 2022; second-hand). Okavango delta-scale upscaling: ~36 in 2018 and ~4.8 in 2019 (derived from Helfter 2022). Five independent sites or data sets. Typical value = median of site centrals. The high end (63.1) conflicts with 36.3 for the same tower-year.

Per mean-annual flooded area, annual regional budgets. Mainstem Solimoes-Amazon floodplain mosaic ~40 per 42,700 km2 mean flooded area (Melack 2022, restating Melack 2004). Pantanal 54 per 61,588 km2 average 2004 flooded area; drought year, open water plus floating macrophytes, rooted vegetation excluded; median-based alternative 28 (Marani 2007). Orinoco fringing floodplain plus upper delta: 114 mg/d per time-weighted mean wetted area (5,200 km2), which gives 41.6 read as an annual mean and 33 from the paper's own Tg total (Smith 2000). South American savanna floodplains 96, assuming Amazon high-water macrophyte rates (Melack 2004 via Marani 2007; secondary). Satellite-constrained model: Amazon 141 per annual-mean flooded area (Bloom 2012; level anchored to an IPCC global total; left out of the range).

Per maximum or mapped floodplain/wetland extent, annual. Orinoco 12.1 per 14,000 km2 total floodplain; this is about the maximum extent, and standing water shrinks to ~6% of maximum by March (Smith 2000). Amazon lowland 42.4-49.6 per 0.84 Mkm2 mapped wetland (Hess). This bottom-up total includes tree stems, open water, macrophytes and 0.4-0.6 Tg of river channel; without trees it is 24.4 (Pangala 2017). Inventory prior, not measured and excluded from the range: alluvial 0.03 g/d x 180 d = 5.4 (Matthews 1987). The same Orinoco data give 33-42 per mean wetted area, so changing the denominator alone shifts the value ~3x. No single central value is defensible.

Per flooded area (ground or water surface) during inundation, in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. These are not annual values, so the g fields are null. Ecosystem totals incl. tree stems: Amazon flooded-forest plots 266-324; 295-353 with in-plot macrophytes; stems alone 135-193 (Pangala 2017). Solimoes-Amazon: flooded-forest water surface 58, or 203 with stems; floating macrophytes 118; floodplain lakes 42 (Melack 2022 Table 1, from Barbosa 2021). Pantanal flooded-forest EC 150.7 in the flooded phase vs 2.7 in the aerobic phase (Dalmagro 2019). Amazon mainstem campaigns: macrophytes 240.7, flooded-forest surface 69.4; Manaus lakes grass 214, forest 150 (Ringeval 2014). Pantanal floating chambers 142 (Marani 2007). Pantropical floodplain and flooded-forest chamber entries: median 174.5, study means 2.4-970 (Sjogersten 2014 Table 4). Negro interfluvial flooded 77 (Belger via Melack 2022). Flooded-forest water surface only 12-55 (Gauci 2021 via Melack 2022). Llanos de Moxos seasonal plains 168 +/- 50 per area overflown, late wet season (France 2022). Okavango floodplain soil gradient ~62 (2.61 mg/h; Gondwe 2021). Typical ~150 mg/d; study means span ~12-324 mg/d. Model priors: Fung 1991 200; Matthews 1987 30; WMEM alluvial 155-201 over the production season (Cao 1996).

table.kind: floodplain (frequently inundated low habitats / seasonally inundated marsh)
table.basis: Per wetland area (per area of the flood-prone habitat), annual, dry periods included. Ogeechee River floodplain swamp, Georgia 32N: low habitats 22.7 (Pulliam 1993, abstract only); modelled long-term mean 36 per low-habitat area, WFP 22 to EFP 45 (Pulliam 1992). Intermittently flooded zones of created riparian marshes, Ohio: 16.8, derived as 30% of 56 (Altor 2006). Poyang Lake floodplain Carex meadow (29N, subtropical): 21 +/- 6, of which 86% is emitted in the flood period (Hu 2016). Sanjiang seasonally inundated wetland 5.8 (3.4-8.2) (Song 2009, abstract only). Four independent sites (Pulliam 1992 and 1993 are the same floodplain).

table.kind: floodplain (whole floodplain incl. rarely flooded higher ground)
table.basis: Per total floodplain area (about the maximum inundable area), annual. Ogeechee: 27 g C m-2 yr-1 per low-habitat area x 0.33 (low habitats' share of the floodplain) x 16/12 = ~12 (derived from Pulliam 1992). Supporting statement: >90% of floodplain CH4 comes from the 30% most frequently inundated (Pulliam 1993). Single floodplain.

table.kind: floodplain (short-hydroperiod meadow / grassland on mineral soil)
table.basis: Per wetland area, annual. UK floodplain hay meadow: 1.14 (0.8-1.5), upscaled from mesocosm emission factors x modelled anoxic days; flood-onset hot moments not captured, so likely a lower bound (Peacock 2024). Austrian Morava floodplain grassland: EC 2.13 in the wet year 2024; may include CH4 from grazing horses and cattle (Lindenberger 2026). Virginia short-hydroperiod floodplain: 'near zero', no number given (Batson 2015, abstract only).

table.kind: floodplain (seasonally inundated riverine, incl. floodplain water bodies)
table.basis: Per flooded area or water surface during flooding, in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual, so the g fields are null. Intermittently flooded marsh zones, growing season ~112 (3.5 mg C/h), against ~256 in permanently inundated zones (Altor 2006). Poyang flood period ~106 (4426 ug/h, Hu 2011 via Hu 2016). Ogeechee warm-season rates 84-157, probably CH4-C (Pulliam 1992). Ephemeral floodplain wetland, single peak 654 (Boon 1997). Danube floodplain waters, diffusive only per water surface, 27-336 by phase and connectivity (Sieczko 2016). Floodplain oxbows 21 (connected) to 507 (isolated) per water surface (Lew 2025). Seasonally inundated depressional forested wetlands, diffusive only 21.8, used as an analogue (Hondula 2021). Riverside medians 10.6-2742 (Sha 2011; extreme). Typical ~110 mg/d; typical study means 21-654 mg/d.

table.kind: floodplain / marsh (river floodplain, delta, lake or stream margin; BAWLD Marsh, Olefeldt Littoral)
table.basis: Per class area, warm-season or summer daily flux in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual; do not multiply by 365, so the g fields are null. BAWLD Marsh (defined as on floodplains, deltas and lake margins, with both flooded and dry periods): median 106, IQR 70.5-200, mean 171.6, 33 site-years, mean water table +2 cm (Kuhn 2021). Littoral (lake or stream edge): median 89 (58.3-112.4) (Olefeldt 2013). Indigirka arctic floodplain summer chambers: mean 300 (wet sites 562, dry 38), measured on 4 days while NOT inundated, against 103 on the adjacent terrace tundra (van Huissteden 2005). Olefeldt 2021 ranks Marsh highest among the BAWLD classes.

Per wetland area, annual, recomputed from the Treat 2018 dataset. Boreal/taiga marsh: median 23.5, IQR 10.7-49.0, n=21; 11 of the rows are Lake Vesijarvi littoral reed marsh; measured-only median 39.1. Tundra marsh (Lena Delta, 72N): 5.2 (3.0-8.7), n=4, none measured. This overlaps the floodplain/marsh class above, because boreal-arctic syntheses do not separate marsh from floodplain.

table.kind: marsh (freshwater, mostly permanently inundated; includes managed impoundments)
table.basis: Per wetland area (tower footprint or site), annual. Syntheses: temperate marsh median 78 (95% CI 63-145) (Treat 2018); FLUXNET-CH4 freshwater marsh median 57.6 (Knox 2019); marsh class mean 54.4 over 10 sites (Delwiche 2021). Sites: Sanjiang permanently inundated 52.5 (43.2-61.9) (Song 2009); diked Lake Erie marsh 66.3 (Chu 2014); Sacramento restored marshes 51.6-70.7 (Knox 2015) and 36.9-84.5 over 14 site-years, median ~65 (Hemes 2018); Mississippi Delta tidal freshwater marsh, 29.9N, 62.3 (Holm 2016); Old Woman Creek reference marsh 76 (Mitsch 2012) with a site maximum of 153.2 (Knox 2019); created riverine flow-through marshes 17.3-62.7, ~40 central (Mitsch 2012); permanently inundated zone of a created marsh 56 (Altor 2006). Typical ~ median of site centrals (62) and synthesis values (54-78). Excluded: Typha patch 292.5, a growing-season rate (Rey-Sanchez 2018).

table.kind: marsh / herbaceous swamp (permanent papyrus or emergent)
table.basis: Per wetland area (tower footprint), annual. Okavango Guma Lagoon papyrus mat: 115.9 in 2018 and 122.1 in 2019, not affected by the drought (Helfter 2021). The seasonal range of monthly flux is 100-640 mg/d (Helfter 2022). FLUXNET-CH4 processing of the same tower gives 68.9 from a 228-day partial-year sum, which the paper calls an underestimate (Delwiche 2021). Negro interfluvial Cuini, permanently flooded to <=0.6 m: 107.6 (Belger data via Ringeval 2014). Inventory prior for non-forested swamp: 0.12 g/d x 180 d = 21.6 (Matthews 1987; not in range). Two sites.

Per wetland area, annual. Treat 2018 dataset temperate swamp: median 4.0 (IQR 1.16-35.9, n=19); measured-only median 17.0 (n=13). Latitudes are 30-57N, so the set probably includes floodplain swamps. Newport News permanently flooded swamp: 43.7 (+/-1 SE 35.9-51.5); bank site 41.4 (Wilson 1989, abstract only). Instantaneous chamber mean for temperate and subtropical swamps: 46.8 mg/d (Turetsky 2014). Tree stems add up to 27% of seasonal flux in a temperate forested mire (Pangala 2015). Not used: FLUXNET-CH4 swamp class 35.2, which mixes tropical towers (Delwiche 2021); inventory prior 10.5 (Matthews 1987). Typical = the measured-only median.

Per wetland area, annual: Treat 2018 dataset boreal swamp median 3.2 (IQR 3.1-4.6, n=11). None of the 11 rows is a measured annual, and all come from essentially one location at 49N. Instantaneous chamber mean for boreal swamps: 2.6 mg/d (Turetsky 2014).

table.kind: swamp forest (mineral soil, not peat, not riverine floodplain)
table.basis: No measured annual value per area. Congo swamp forest ~67-69, derived by dividing a modelled basin total by the swamp-forest extent (Byrne 2026, citing Zou 2022). The area basis is uncertain and may include non-flooded pixels. WMEM model annual mean for forested swamps, 83% of them tropical: 38.2 per inundated area (Cao 1996). Inventory prior: 0.07 g/d x 180 d = 12.6 (Matthews 1987). The only chamber value is a campaign mean for Congo flooded forest, 106 mg/d (4.41 mg/h; Tathy 1992 via Sjogersten 2014).

Per wetland area (EC tower footprint), annual. Sarawak MY-MLM: 12.3 (10-14.4); the most reliable variants give 13.1-14.4 (Wong 2018); 12.7 in Delwiche 2021. Sumatra undrained peat forest: 9.1 (8.2-10) (Deshmukh 2020). Palangkaraya ID-PAG: ~0.12 (from tables; the text prints 0.013) (Delwiche 2021). Peruvian Mauritia palm peatland EC: 29.3 (Griffis 2020 via Melack 2022). Soil-only and tree-inclusive plot values from SE Asia are lower: chambers 0.024-<1.36 (Melling 2005 and Jauhiainen 2005 via Wong 2018); Kalimantan ecosystem value incl. trees 0.4-1.2 as a wet-season upper bound (Pangala 2013). Upper bound at high water: <=26 if 3 mg/h held all year (Couwenberg 2010). Excluded: 53.4, from chamber means annualized over the whole year (Sjogersten 2014). Water tables fall 30-44 cm below the surface in the dry season, so these sites are not permanently flooded. Typical = median of the EC sites.

Per ground area, campaign-mean daily flux in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual, so the g fields are null. The distribution is bimodal. SE Asian forested peat: median 15.2 (0.07-29) from 10 study means, typically <48 (<2 mg/h) (Sjogersten 2014); <=72 at high water (Couwenberg 2010); Kalimantan ecosystem incl. trees 1.1-3.3 in the wet season (Pangala 2013); MY-MLM EC in the early wet season ~32 (Tang 2018). Neotropical peat: Peru 48-336 (Teh, del Aguila-Pasquel, Winton via Melack 2022); Panama study means 346-744, where one open-peatland entry is internally inconsistent (Sjogersten 2014).

Per wetland area, annual. Treat 2018 dataset: boreal bog median 5.6 (IQR 3.2-13.1, n=110; measured-only 6.8); tundra bog 0.9 (measured-only 0.21). The paper warns that estimates built from growing-season data overestimate bogs by ~400%. FLUXNET-CH4 bog class mean 14.0 (7 sites, mostly boreal and temperate; Delwiche 2021). Inventory prior 0.2 g/d x 100 d = 20 (Matthews 1987; not in range).

Per class area, warm-season daily flux in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual, so the g fields are null. BAWLD Bog median 24.55 (IQR 6.92-57.35); Permafrost Bog 2.32 (0-6.9) (Kuhn 2021). Bog median 23.0 (5.6-83), 11 of 35 sites recently thawed (Olefeldt 2013). Pooled instantaneous bog median 25.8, subarctic to temperate (Turetsky 2014).

Per wetland area, annual. Treat 2018 dataset temperate bog: median 6.1 (IQR 1.9-23.0, n=51; measured-only 5.7). Mer Bleue, Ontario: 6-year mean 4.9 (+/-1 SD 4.3-5.6) (Roulet 2007), and 5-25 whole-bog annual (Moore 2011). Inventory prior 0.2 g/d x 150 d = 30 (Matthews 1987; not in range).

Per wetland area, annual, from the Treat 2018 dataset. Boreal fen: median 8.4 (IQR 4.4-18.7, n=227); measured-only 17.6; the paper says estimated annuals run ~40% below measured ones for fens. Tundra fen: 9.9 (6.2-25.4). Not in range: FLUXNET-CH4 fen class mean 27.3, from 8 sites in mixed climates (Delwiche 2021).

Per class area, warm-season daily flux in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual, so the g fields are null. BAWLD Fen median 54 (IQR 20-107.2) (Kuhn 2021). Fen 37.1 (11.5-95) and permafrost fen 75.8 (41.7-147.3) (Olefeldt 2013). Pooled instantaneous medians: poor fen 51.3, rich fen 44.5 (Turetsky 2014).

Per wetland area, annual: Treat 2018 dataset temperate fen median 23.8 (IQR 8.7-40.5, n=37; measured-only 39.7). Excluded as a disturbed state: a rewetted fen that became permanently inundated shallow water, post-rewetting mean ~120 with a 305 peak (Antonijevic 2023).

Per wetland area (tower footprint), annual. FLUXNET-CH4 wet tundra class mean 5.07 +/- 2.4 SD, 11 sites / 39 site-years (Delwiche 2021). Tundra-biome wetlands median 3.9 (IQR 2.4-5.6) (Knox 2019; same network). All tundra wetlands 6.2 (Treat 2018). Annual EC sums north of 20N skip winter gaps longer than 2 months, so they are underestimates.

Per class area, warm-season daily flux in mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Not annual, so the g fields are null. BAWLD Tundra Wetland median 65 (IQR 34-99.3) (Kuhn 2021). Wet tundra 64.5 (31.9-100.6) (Olefeldt 2013). Indigirka terrace tundra 103 in summer, wet sites 172 (van Huissteden 2005). Permafrost sites, all types: mean 47.9 vs 96.8 at permafrost-free sites, instantaneous (Turetsky 2014).

Per wetland area (tower footprint), annual. FLUXNET-CH4 tropical band (<20 deg): 32.7 +/- 27.6 SD, n=9 site-years mixing peat forests, the Pantanal flooded forest and Okavango swamp and floodplain; the paper says this is not different from other bands because of small n (Delwiche 2021). Tropical/subtropical: 57.6 (IQR 26.7-62.4) from only 3 site-years, two of them Louisiana marshes (Knox 2019). Chamber syntheses annualized over the whole year, excluded because biased high for seasonal systems: mineral soils 72, organic soils 53.4 (Sjogersten 2014).

Per wetland area, annual. FLUXNET-CH4 temperate: median 36.5 (IQR 13.3-63.1, 47 site-years; includes 3 salt-marsh sites) (Knox 2019). 40-60N mean 39.6; subtropical 20-40 deg mean 53.5 (Delwiche 2021). All temperate wetland types incl. bogs 13.3 (Treat 2018).

Per wetland area, annual. FLUXNET-CH4: boreal median 12.7 (IQR 8.0-15.1), tundra 3.9 (2.4-5.6) (Knox 2019); >60N mean 11.6 (Delwiche 2021). Treat 2018: boreal 7.2, tundra 6.2. Permafrost-free sites emit 2.5x permafrost sites (6.9 vs 2.7; Treat 2018).

table.kind: all wetland types (process-model ensembles, not observations)
table.basis: Model emission divided by model wetland area. WETCHIMP, 30S-30N, per mean annual MAXIMUM wetland area: median of 7 models 32.1, from 10.2 (SDGVM) to 88.5 (IAP-RAS); CLM4Me 51.5, partly from the CLM4 tropical NPP bias, with rice unmasked (Melton 2013). GCP ensemble, tropical area-weighted monthly flux 5.2-8.2 g/month x 12 = 62.4-98.4 (Poulter 2017). Models with smaller wetland area tend to simulate higher per-area flux (Melton 2013).

table.kind: all wetland types (process-model ensembles, not observations)
table.basis: Model emission divided by model wetland area. WETCHIMP >35N, per annual maximum area: median of 8 models 10.3 (2.3-20.9); CLM4Me 12.2 (Melton 2013). GCP boreal: 0.7-3.1 g/month x 12 = 8.4-37.2 (Poulter 2017). LPJ-WHyMe northern peatlands: prior 18.8-25.1 per 2.05 Mkm2 peatland; ~13.8 after inversion (Spahni 2011).

table.kind: all wetland types incl. floodplains (GCP definition; process-model ensembles)
table.basis: Prognostic model emissions divided by area. 159 [119-203] Tg / WAD2M annual-mean 7.9 Mkm2 = 20.1 (15.1-25.7); per peak-season area of 13.6 Mkm2 it is 11.7 (Saunois 2025). 158 Tg / 8.0 Mkm2 = 19.8 (Zhang 2025). Area-weighted monthly flux 2.7-3.9 g/month x 12 = 32.4-46.8 (Poulter 2017). The range 15.1-25.7 is not a range of per-model per-area fluxes, because each model has its own area.

ordering.statement: Tropical, per flooded area while inundated: permanent herbaceous (papyrus) swamp >= seasonal floodplain habitats >> SE Asian peat swamp forest.
ordering.support: Papyrus swamp averages ~320-335 mg/d over the whole year (115.9-122.1 g/yr; Helfter 2021) and has a seasonal range of 100-640 mg/d (Helfter 2022). Floodplain rates during the flooded phase are 12-324 mg/d, typical ~150. Examples: EC flooded phase 150.7 (Dalmagro 2019); ecosystem incl. stems 266-324 (Pangala 2017); macrophytes 118-241 (Melack 2022; Ringeval 2014). SE Asian peat swamp: EC 9.1-12.7 g/yr, i.e. ~25-35 mg/d (Deshmukh 2020; Wong 2018); soil chambers typically <48 mg/d (Sjogersten 2014). Mechanisms: mineral-soil wetlands emit more than organic-soil wetlands (8.22 vs 6.10 mg/h; Sjogersten 2014). SE Asian peat is limited by low pH, strong CH4 oxidation and recalcitrant lignin-rich C (Pangala 2017; Wong 2018). Amazon floodplain trees vent soil CH4, with stems 44-65% of plot flux (Pangala 2017). Exception: Neotropical peat, where chamber means are 48-744 mg/d and palm-peat EC is 29.3 g/yr (Melack 2022; Sjogersten 2014).

ordering.statement: Tropical, per wetland (land) area per year: seasonal floodplain < permanent herbaceous swamp, by ~3x in a normal year and ~14x in a drought year. Flood duration sets the gap.
ordering.support: Okavango towers: seasonal floodplain 36.3 vs papyrus 115.9 g/yr in 2018, and 8.7 vs 122.1 in the 2019 drought. The floodplain decrease is attributed to soil drying and oxygenation (Helfter 2021). Permanent vegetated wetlands gave 63% (2018) and 97% (2019) of delta emission from 24% of the area (Helfter 2022). Flooding works as an on-off switch: flux drops ~50-fold after recession (0.113 vs 0.002 g C/d), and annual flux varies mainly with flood duration (Dalmagro 2019). Derived check: 150.7 mg/d x 179 flooded days = 27 g, against 25.3 measured. Exposed floodplain soil is ~0 (+/-1 mg/d; Gauci 2021 via Melack 2022). Caveat: FLUXNET-CH4 processing of the same two towers gives 63.1 vs >=68.9 (the latter from a partial year), almost equal (Delwiche 2021). The size of the gap is therefore uncertain; its sign is not.

ordering.statement: Tropical, per land area per year: seasonal floodplain (typical ~24, 5-63) >= SE Asian peat swamp (0.1-14). Neotropical palm peat (29.3) is comparable to floodplains. Drought years bring floodplains down to the peat-swamp level.
ordering.support: Floodplain site values: 25.3 (Dalmagro 2019), 36.3 and 8.7 (Helfter 2021), 10.4-10.7 (Ringeval 2014), 51.4 (Amaral 2026). Peat swamp: 12.3 (Wong 2018), 9.1 (Deshmukh 2020), ~0.1 (Delwiche 2021 ID-PAG), 29.3 (Melack 2022 citing Griffis 2020). Tropical peat-swamp water tables drop 30-44 cm below the surface in the dry season (Wong 2018; Deshmukh 2020), and flux there tracks the water table rather than temperature (Wong 2018).

ordering.statement: Theory on per-inundated-area rates for seasonal vs permanent flooding points both ways. Observations favour permanent > seasonal on an annual per-land-area basis, but the evidence per flooded area during the flood itself is mixed.
ordering.support: Lowers the seasonal rate: CLM4Me factor S (Riley 2011), where dry-season aerobic decomposition keeps the equilibrium C stock small, so seasonally inundated soil emits less per inundated area even in the wet season. S ranges from beta=0.2 (brief flooding) to 1 (permanent), with a production-weighted global mean of 0.95. Re-oxidized electron acceptors delay methanogenesis after re-flooding (Bridgham 2013; Cui 2024: lag 17 +/- 11 d, transition flux 5x below steady wet). Raises the seasonal rate: litter that accumulates in the dry season fuels a peak at rising water that declines before peak water (Bloom 2012; Gloor 2021 Pantanal; Barbosa 2020, where macrophytes on exposed sediment decompose on reflooding). Hondula 2021: inundation extent and duration, not depth, drive emissions.

ordering.statement: Temperate, per wetland area per year: permanent marsh (~60; 17-153) > frequently inundated floodplain low habitats (~21; 6-45) ~ fen (~24) > bog (~5.5) ~ swamp (4-17; permanently flooded swamp 44) > short-hydroperiod floodplain meadow or grassland (1-2).
ordering.support: Paired sites: permanently inundated 52.5 vs seasonally inundated 5.8 (9x; Song 2009). Permanent zone 56 vs intermittent zones 16.8 (3.3x); growing season 256 vs 112 mg/d (Altor 2006). Inundated 120 vs non-inundated 4 in a rewetted fen, ~28-31x (Antonijevic 2023). >90% of floodplain flux comes from the 30% most frequently inundated (Pulliam 1993). Mechanisms: about half of the CH4 entering floodwater is oxidized in the water column, and emission stops below ~15 C soil temperature, so cold-season floods emit little (Pulliam 1993). Water-table fluctuation zones host oxidation hotspots (Cui 2024, hedged). Alternative electron acceptors are regenerated between floods (Bridgham 2013; Cui 2024). Syntheses: flooded, nutrient-rich marshes and fens >= bogs (Treat 2018); marsh highest in FLUXNET-CH4 (Knox 2019).

ordering.statement: Temperate conditions under which a floodplain matches or exceeds permanent wetland: fresh litter from newly flooded vegetation, warm-season flooding, isolated (stagnant) floodplain waters, or sulfate-rich permanent water.
ordering.support: Newly flooded vegetated land: fresh litter drove elevated emissions for years, peaking at 229 g C (Antonijevic 2023). Ephemeral floodplain wetlands at peak matched permanent SE Australian wetlands, and emission began within 3-6 days of a summer flood but was negligible after autumn or winter floods (Boon 1997). Isolated floodplain waters and oxbows emit more than connected ones (Sieczko 2016; Lew 2025: 507 vs 21 mg/d), because connection flushes CH4 to the river. Temporary prairie potholes respond more strongly than sulfate-rich permanent ones (Bansal 2016). Pulsing lowers emission in deep zones: steady-flow year ~2x the pulsed year (Altor 2008; Mitsch 2012). Flood-deposited particulate organic matter raises floodplain flux above adjacent wetlands (Cui 2024 citing van Huissteden 2005).

ordering.statement: Boreal-arctic, warm-season flux per class area: floodplain/marsh/littoral is the highest class, so here floodplain-type wetlands exceed permanent peatlands. Order: Marsh (106 mg/d) >= littoral (89) > wet tundra (65) ~ fen (54; permafrost fen 76) > bog (24.5) > permafrost bog (2.3).
ordering.support: Kuhn 2021 and Olefeldt 2013 medians. Olefeldt 2021 ranks the classes Permafrost Bogs < Bogs < Fens = Tundra Wetlands < Marshes. Mechanisms: minerotrophic, nutrient-rich wetlands with dynamic hydrology on floodplains and deltas (Kuhn 2021); higher NPP, sedge-mediated transport and flood-deposited POM (van Huissteden 2005: floodplain 300 vs terrace tundra 103 mg/d). Condition: the van Huissteden floodplain was measured while not inundated, and the authors say inundated similar vegetation in Alaska gives only 1.6-4.0 mg/h. Wet-sedge tundra and floodplain sedge sites did not differ significantly.

ordering.statement: Boreal-arctic annual per area: boreal marsh (23.5) > fen (8.4) > bog (5.6) > swamp (3.2). In the tundra biome the marsh advantage flips: fen (9.9) > marsh (5.2, Lena Delta, estimated) > bog (0.9).
ordering.support: Treat 2018 dataset medians. Measured-only medians are higher: boreal marsh 39.1, boreal fen 17.6. Marshes and shallow waters have the smallest non-growing-season share of annual flux; the share is 42% in tundra, 20% in temperate and 16% in boreal sites (Treat 2018). Warm-season rates therefore need the smallest winter add-on for marsh. Permafrost-free sites emit 2.5x permafrost sites (Treat 2018).

ordering.statement: Across climates, tower data do not show tropical > temperate per area. Process models put tropical per-area flux well above tower values and above extratropical per-area flux by 4-7x.
ordering.support: FLUXNET-CH4 annual per area: tropical 32.7, temperate 39.6, subtropical 53.5, northern 11.6 g CH4 (Delwiche 2021). Mean annual air temperature explains 51% of between-site variance, and the tropical band is not significantly different from the others (n=9 site-years). Models: GCP tropical 62-98 (Poulter 2017); CLM4Me tropical 51.5 vs extratropical 12.2, a 4.2x ratio (Melton 2013); LPJ-WSL tropical scaling factor 7x boreal (Hodson 2011); ORCHIDEE tropical a0 ~5x boreal (Ringeval 2010). Models with smaller wetland area simulate higher per-area flux, and CLM4Me's tropical intensity partly reflects an NPP bias (Melton 2013).

ordering.statement: Flood depth, duration and oxygen decide whether a floodplain ranks high or low. Deep, long, anoxic flooding gives a high rate; shallow, short, oxic or flushed flooding gives a low one.
ordering.support: Orinoco: shallow, short flooding with oxic water over sediment gives ~2-3x lower per-area flux than the Amazon (Smith 2000). Deeper water increases oxidation in LPX, and lateral inflow of oxygen-rich river water near channels is hypothesized to lower flux (Ringeval 2014). Water-column oxidation in floodplain lakes runs ~1-175 mg m-3 d-1 and rises with O2 (Melack 2022 citing Barbosa 2018). Deep flooding inhibits flux through slow diffusion, less plant C input and electron acceptors in moving water (Turetsky 2014). Opposing results: tropical CH4 is largest from water >40 cm deep (Byrne 2026 citing Zou 2022), and marsh flux rises with standing-water depth through inundated litter (Ding 2003). Historical priors disagree completely: alluvial formations lowest at 0.03 g/d vs bogs 0.2 (Matthews 1987), but alluvial highest at 0.20 vs forested swamp 0.07 (Fung 1991).

ordering.statement: Theoretical range for floodplain annual flux per land area (derived arithmetic): annual ~= flooded-phase rate x flooded days, plus ~0 in the dry phase. With observed flooded-phase rates of 30-324 mg/d and 90-270 flooded days, this gives ~2.7-87 g CH4 m-2 yr-1. Observed site values (4.8-63 tropical; 1-45 temperate) fall inside that envelope.
ordering.support: Dry-phase flux is ~0: 2.7 mg/d at BR-Npw (Dalmagro 2019); +/-1 mg/d for exposed floodplain soil (Gauci 2021 via Melack 2022). Flooded-phase rates come from the tropical and temperate flooded-period rows. The BR-Npw closure check gives 27 g computed vs 25.3 measured. The flooded-day bounds are illustrative. The 3-6 month flooding of Okavango seasonal swamps (Helfter 2021) and the 179 d mean at BR-Npw (Dalmagro 2019) lie inside them.

ordering.statement: Theoretical range for permanent wetlands per wetland area per year spans roughly three orders of magnitude. SE Asian undrained peat ~0.1-14. Bogs 1-14 (temperate up to 25). Fens 4-40. Boreal marsh 3-49. Temperate marsh 17-153. Tropical papyrus swamp 69-122. Temperate permanently flooded swamp ~44.
ordering.support: Compiled from the table rows: Delwiche 2021, Wong 2018, Deshmukh 2020, Treat 2018, Roulet 2007, Moore 2011, Knox 2019, Song 2009, Chu 2014, Hemes 2018, Mitsch 2012, Helfter 2021, Wilson 1989.

ordering.statement: Consistency bound for a model's annual rate per inundated area in tropical floodplains (derived). Verified observational values per mean flooded area are 28-54, or 96 from one secondary source assuming macrophyte rates. The highest measured flooded-phase ecosystem rate (324 mg/d incl. stems) gives 118 g only if held all 365 days. A model rate above ~120 g CH4 m-2 yr-1 per inundated area therefore exceeds every observational constraint, and exceeds the satellite-anchored model estimate of 141 once it passes that value.
ordering.support: Melack 2022; Marani 2007; Smith 2000; Pangala 2017 (324 x 365 = 118); Bloom 2012 (141 per annual-mean flooded area). Tropical tower annual per footprint: 32.7 (Delwiche 2021).

basis_caveats: Floodplain regional budgets change about threefold with the choice of denominator. The Orinoco is 12.1 per total floodplain area (about the maximum extent) but 33-42 per time-weighted mean wetted area (Smith 2000). The Amazon value of 40 uses the mean-annual flooded area of 42,700 km2 (Melack 2022). The Pantanal value of 54 uses the average 2004 flooded area (Marani 2007). Pangala 2017's 42-50 uses the mapped maximum wetland area. A model that computes flux per instantaneous inundated fraction must be compared with the per-mean-flooded-area values. It must not be compared with values per maximum area or per wetland area.

Chamber syntheses (Turetsky 2014, Kuhn 2021, Olefeldt 2013) give warm-season or instantaneous daily fluxes per class area. Do not multiply them by 365. The non-growing season adds 16% (boreal) to 42% (tundra) of annual flux, and less in marshes (Treat 2018). Warm-season medians are 1.6-4.7x the year-round mean implied by the matching annual values: bog 24.5 vs 15.3, fen 54 vs 22.9, marsh 106 vs 64, wet tundra 65 vs 13.9 mg/d (derived).

EC footprints and chamber placement are biased toward wet source areas. The Nxaraga footprint includes a reed-fringed river channel. Applying a 200 m footprint filter cuts the local budget by 34% in 2018 and 78% in 2019, and the authors call the upscaled seasonal budgets likely overestimates (Helfter 2022). Inundated zones supply 83-99% of emission in seasonally inundated wetlands. Using the variable inundated area gives 57-74% of the fixed-area estimate (Hondula 2021).

Treat 2018 annual values mix measured, estimated (from growing-season data) and modelled rows. Estimates overestimate bogs by ~400% and shallow water by ~170%, and underestimate fens by ~40%. Measured-only medians differ strongly from the pooled medians: boreal fen 17.6 vs 8.4; temperate swamp 17 vs 4; boreal marsh 39 vs 23.5. For temperate marsh, Treat's 78 g and Knox's quotation of Treat as 49.6 g C (66 g CH4) conflict, and the conflict cannot be resolved from the printed values.

FLUXNET-CH4 annual sums north of 20N omit winter gaps longer than 2 months, so they are underestimates. The BW-GUM total is a 228-day partial year. Knox 2019 reports in g C, which needs x16/12. Its temperate 'Wetlands' class includes salt marshes, and its tropical/subtropical class is 3 site-years, two of them in Louisiana (Delwiche 2021; Knox 2019).

Water-surface diffusive fluxes (Sieczko 2016, Hondula 2021, Gauci 2021, Dalmagro 2018) are lower bounds on total emission. Floating or soil chambers miss tree stems. Stems carry 44-65% of flux in Amazon floodplain plots (Pangala 2017) and 62-87% in a Kalimantan peat swamp (Pangala 2013). Non-flooded riparian trees add emission outside the inundated area: 2.2-3.6 Tg in the Amazon (Gauci 2022).
Sjogersten 2014 annualizes campaign means as if they held all year (8.22 mg/h x 8760 h = 72 g). This is biased high for seasonal floodplains, and the 91.6 Tg upscaling depends on it.

Aircraft and regional values are per total region area and include non-wetland sources. They are not per-wetland rates: Basso 2021 Amazonia 4.6, Pangala 2017 aircraft 4-22, Gloor 2021 via Melack 2022 Pantanal 18.3, Li 2024 Pantanal dry season per domain area, Amaral 2026 Llanos del Orinoco 6.4-10.4 (total of all sources).

Many temperate 'permanent marsh' towers are impounded or managed to stay flooded all year: Chu 2014 diked marsh, Knox 2015 and Hemes 2018 restored Sacramento marshes, Mitsch 2012 and Altor 2006 pumped created marshes. Their values describe engineered permanent inundation, not natural hydroperiods.
van Huissteden 2005 is an unweighted chamber mean from 4 July days while the floodplain was not inundated, excluding one 559 mg/h outlier. It is not an annual value and not a per-flooded-area value.

GCP defines wetlands to include seasonal and permanent floodplains, and to exclude open water without emergent macrophytes. The 159 Tg wetland total has not had the 23 Tg double-counting correction applied (Saunois 2025). Floodplain open water (oxbows, floodplain lakes) arguably belongs with inland waters.

Model per-area values depend on the model's own area. A smaller area gives a higher per-area flux (Melton 2013). Values per annual maximum area understate the flux per mean inundated area. Poulter 2017's monthly x 12 values carry no season weighting.

Latitude and climate labels: Holm 2016 (29.9N), Poyang (29N), Pulliam (32N) and the Louisiana towers sit at the model's 30-degree tropical boundary. Turetsky 2014 has no tropical sites; its 'subtropical' row is 2 sites.
Unit conversions: g C x 16/12 = g CH4; mg/h x 24 = mg/d; mg/d x 0.365 = g/yr only if the rate holds all year. Tg per 10^6 km2 = g m-2.
gaps: Tropical floodplain annual values per land area rest on only two EC towers (BR-Npw, BW-Nxr), and they disagree across processing (36.3 vs 63.1 for the same tower-year). There is only one permanent herbaceous tropical tower (BW-Gum). The whole tropical tower set is 9 site-years.

There is no measured annual per-area value for tropical mineral-soil swamp forest outside riverine floodplains, e.g. the Congo Cuvette. The only inputs are one chamber campaign mean and a modelled total divided by an uncertain area.

No boreal-arctic floodplain has an annual per-flooded-area or per-land-area measurement. The data are summer chamber snapshots on non-inundated sites (van Huissteden 2005) and estimated or modelled Lena Delta marsh rows (Treat 2018).

Temperate natural river-floodplain annual values come from one Georgia floodplain (Pulliam, abstract-level for 1993), created marshes (Altor), one lake floodplain (Poyang) and grassland/meadow sites. There is no EC tower on a natural temperate floodplain forest. No temperate floodplain has an annual value per maximum inundated area except the one derived from Pulliam 1992.

Only a few sites pair floodplain and permanent wetland within one area: Okavango (tropical), Sanjiang (Song 2009), created Ohio marshes (Altor 2006), a rewetted fen (Antonijevic 2023) and Indigirka (van Huissteden 2005). No pair exists in the Amazon or in the boreal zone.

No observation tests the theoretical per-inundated-area contrast between seasonal and permanent flooding directly: the CLM4Me S factor, beta = 0.2 to 1 (Riley 2011), against the dry-season litter pulse (Bloom 2012).
Neotropical peat has a single EC value (Griffis 2020, cited second-hand via Melack 2022). Chamber means there span 48-744 mg/d, with one internally inconsistent entry.
Southern-hemisphere temperate floodplains are represented only by one peak value (Boon 1997).
No verified source gives lateral CH4 export from floodplains to rivers as a per-area term (Zhang 2025 notes that models omit it).

Several rows rest on abstracts only, full text not read: Pulliam 1993, Wilson 1989, Song 2009, Altor 2006 and 2008, Couwenberg 2010, Yu 2008, Sha 2011, Ding 2003, Batson 2015, Roulet 2007. Their areal basis, method and the meaning of their ± values are not confirmed.
The Treat 2018 temperate-marsh value (78 g CH4) conflicts with Knox 2019's citation of it (49.6 g C), and the primary full text is not open, so the conflict cannot be resolved.

critic:
Critique of the floodplain vs permanent-wetland CH4 synthesis: what is missing or weak

1. Major syntheses and primary campaigns not used
- Aselmann and Crutzen 1989 and Bartlett and Harriss 1993 were not read. They are the classic per-type tables for floodplain, marsh, swamp, bog and fen.
- The Amazon ABLE campaigns were not used (Bartlett 1988/1990, Devol 1988/1990, Wassmann 1992, Engle and Melack 2000). They give per-habitat rates at high and low water, and they are the primary base under Melack 2004/2022.
- The Zhang 2025 supplement (area by latitude band) and WetCHARTs (Bloom 2017) are missing. Either would give model per-area flux by band against which our model can be compared directly.

2. Regions not covered
- Congo: no measured annual value per unit area. Borges 2015 was not accessed.
- Sudd, Inner Niger Delta, Zambezi/Barotse, Mekong/Tonle Sap, Ganges-Brahmaputra: none.
- Siberian floodplains: the Ob/Irtysh chamber sets and the Kolyma/Chersky floodplain EC (Kwon 2016, Göckede) are missing. Indigirka rests on 4 summer days measured while the floodplain was not flooded.
- North American deltas (Mackenzie, Peace-Athabasca) and the Atchafalaya: none.
- Chinese floodplain lakes: only Poyang. Dongting, and Sanjiang beyond its abstract, are unread.

3. Mixed bases
- Floodplain rows mix per land area, per mean flooded area and per maximum area.
- Boreal "floodplain" is really the BAWLD marsh class used as a proxy.
- Kuhn 2021 and Olefeldt 2013 come from the same lineage, so they are not independent.
- Temperate "permanent marsh" is mostly impounded or pumped sites.
- Treat 2018 mixes estimated and measured rows.

4. Cells resting on one source
- Temperate whole-floodplain: Pulliam only, partly abstract-level.
- Boreal swamp: one location.
- Boreal marsh annual: Treat only, and 11 of its rows are one lake.
- Tundra marsh: Lena rows that are estimated, not measured.
- Temperate fen: Treat only.
- Tropical papyrus: one tower plus Cuini.
- Tropical swamp forest: no measured annual.

5. Claims that need a second source
- Tropical "permanent > seasonal per land area": rests on the Okavango pair alone, and the gap nearly disappears under FLUXNET-CH4 processing.
- The closure "flooded-phase rate × flooded days = annual": checked only at BR-Npw.
- The ~120 g upper bound: rests on a single Pangala 2017 plot maximum.
- Water-column oxidation of about 50%: Pulliam only.

6. Verification failures
- 33 DOIs were flagged partly_wrong. They include the anchors Treat 2018, Knox 2019, Delwiche 2021, Pangala 2017, Cao 1996 and Ringeval 2014.
- Every number taken from them needs rechecking.

Footnote c and Methods state the extrapolation area (~7.25 × 10^6 km², Amazonia mask). The per-area value is therefore per total regional area, not per wetland or flooded area. As a check, 12.7 mg m−2 d−1 × 7.25e12 m² × 365 d = 33.6 Tg/yr, which matches 33.8. The conversions hold: 12.7 → 4.64, 8.4 → 3.07 and 17.0 → 6.21 g CH4 m−2 yr−1. Low and high are ±1σ from the Monte Carlo analysis. The method field needs two corrections. First, per footnote d, FWTL = FNON-FIRE minus anthropogenic (EDGAR v5, 2010–2015 mean) minus termites (~0.5 mg m−2 d−1), PLUS the upland-soil uptake (~1.0 mg m−2 d−1) added back. The 'Wetland' term is a residual of all remaining non-fire natural sources, and the paper calls it 'attributable mainly to wetlands'. The per-wetland and per-flooded values would be higher. It covers dry-season months only. Author, year and unit are correct, and leaving g/m2/yr null is correct because the value is not annual. Correction: value_low=31.7 and value_high=32.0 are not bounds. They are the two monthly means (May and June/July). The printed uncertainty is ±1 SD, which gives May 18.1-45.3 and June/July 11.8-52.2 mg CH4 m-2 d-1. Overall range at ±1 SD: about 11.8-52.2 mg m-2 d-1. confirmed_rows.quote: Daily fluxes of CH4 determined from the measurements using box models and inverse modeling were between 168 (± 50) and 456 (± 145) mg CH4⋅m-2⋅d-1 for the areas overflown
confirmed_rows.check_note: Crossref matches (France, 2022, PNAS 119(32) e2206345119, 11 authors). I checked the quote against the Crossref abstract and the Europe PMC full text (PMC9371645). It is printed word for word, in mg CH4 m-2 d-1, for 'the areas overflown' in early March 2019 (late wet season). The values are campaign snapshots, not annual rates, so leaving the g/m2/yr fields null is correct. The problem is that 168 and 456 are not the low and high ends of a range for one wetland type. The Results say the box model assumed 'the wetland surface emits at a constant rate per square kilometer' and gave '168 (± 50) ... and 456 (± 145) mg CH4·m−2·d−1 for the areas overflown by Flights A and B, respectively'. The Discussion splits these into 'a seasonally inundated wetland flux from the plains (Flight A)' and 'a more intense flux centered on tree-lined permanently inundated area along the major river channel (Flight B)'. So 168 ± 50 is the seasonal floodplain value. 456 ± 145 comes from the river channel / permanently inundated riverine forest path, so the label 'seasonally flooded savanna floodplain' fits only the lower value. The paper also gives other estimates for the Flight B path: GEOS-Chem inversion 384 ± 48, NAME inversion 156 ± 48 mg m-2 d-1. The flux needed to match GOSAT is ~210 ± 55 (Jan–Mar mean, 2010–2020) and ~355 ± 115 for 2019. All of these are per land area overflown, not per flooded area. The paper also annualizes Flight A, taken as the most representative of the region, using Rio Branco seasonality: ~3.6 Tg CH4/y for the whole ~70,000 km2 region. Dividing gives about 51 g CH4 m-2 yr-1 per region area. The paper does not print that per-area number; I derived it. Naively multiplying by 365 (61 and 166 g m-2 yr-1) would be wrong, because the fluxes are peak-season only.

The paper's own totals do not match it: 0.174 Tg (Table 4) / 5200 km2 = 33.5 g m-2 yr-1, or 32.7 with 0.17 Tg. 7.1 mmol x 5200 km2 x 365 d gives 0.216 Tg, not 0.174. confirmed_rows.check_note: Confirmed. I opened the full text from Europe PMC (PMC12183415, open access). The abstract quote matches the paper word for word. Crossref gives Lew, S., Burandt, P. and Glińska-Lewczuk, K., Environmental Microbiology 27(6), e70127, 2025, so the author and year agree. Table 2 has more precise values (mean ± SD, mg CH4 m-2 day-1): river 32.06 ± 33.49 (N=24), lotic 21.68 ± 13.59 (N=108), semi-lotic 225.42 ± 267.09 (N=144), lentic 506.91 ± 317.68 (N=108), all sites 235.20 ± 302.07. Rounded properly, the lotic value would be 22; the abstract prints 21. How the fluxes were measured: a floating chamber with a Picarro GasScouter CRDS analyser. Each run lasted 3 minutes around midday and was done in triplicate. The method records net emission, meaning diffusion plus any bubbles that entered the chamber. The daily rate is scaled from a single 3-minute window: eCH4 = (C180 − C0)·ρ·0.004·480/0.0615, where 480 is the number of 3-minute intervals in a day. Sampling: 8 seasonal campaigns (winter, May, August, October in each of 2021 and 2022), at 3 points per lake. That gives 10 lakes plus the Łyna River, 11 sites in total, in north-eastern Poland. The paper calls the Table 2 values 'mean annual', but they are means of midday seasonal snapshots, so the row's 'NOT annualized' is right. The method field can be filled with 'floating chamber + CRDS, midday, diffusion plus chamber-captured bubbles'. (2) The Discussion says the lowest recorded value was 75.6 in winter and the highest was 969 in a lentic lake in summer. That minimum cannot apply to all lakes, because the lotic mean is 21.7, so it probably refers to lentic lakes only. The paper does not settle this. If annualized by ×365 (assumes the midday seasonal mean holds all year, which probably biases it high): lotic 7.9, semi-lotic 82.3, lentic 185.0 g CH4 m-2 yr-1. Using the abstract's rounded values gives 7.7, 82.1 and 185.1.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Soils in flooded-forest plots emit about zero or take up CH4 once the water table is below the surface. Floodplain annual flux therefore scales with the duration of inundation.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Exposed floodplain soil ~0 (-1 to +1 mg m-2 d-1) versus tens to hundreds of mg m-2 d-1 when flooded.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Soil CH4 fluxes when the water table was below the surface in these plots were low and often negative, ranging from uptake of ~1 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 to evasion of ~1 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 (Gauci et al., 2021).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Sect. 5.3, p. 10: the quote is exact. Soil flux with the water table below the surface ranged from ~1 mg m-2 d-1 uptake to ~1 mg m-2 d-1 evasion (Gauci et al. 2021, forested floodplain plots). The second sentence, that annual flux scales with inundation duration, is the extractor's inference and is not stated in the source. Sect. 8.1 notes only that Table 1 excludes floodplain soil fluxes during low water.

crossref.title: Challenges Regionalizing Methane Emissions Using Aquatic Environments in the Amazon Basin as Examples

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Water-column CH4 oxidation in Amazon floodplain lakes is large and rises with CH4 concentration and dissolved oxygen.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Oxic, well-mixed water over floodplains lowers net flux.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Barbosa et al. (2018) found that a large fraction of dissolved CH4 was oxidized with volumetric CH4 oxidation rates ranging from ~1 to 175 mg CH4 m−3 d−1 ... CH4 oxidation had a positive relation with CH4 concentration and the presence of dissolved oxygen.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is exact and sits in Sect. 6.1, p. 12: oxidation rates of ~1 to 175 mg CH4 m-3 d-1, positively related to CH4 concentration and the presence of dissolved oxygen. The evidence comes from a single varzea lake (Barbosa et al. 2018), so 'Amazon floodplain lakes' generalizes it. The source does not state 'well-mixed water lowers net flux'. That wording is interpretation.

crossref.title: Challenges Regionalizing Methane Emissions Using Aquatic Environments in the Amazon Basin as Examples

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In Amazon floodplain lakes a large fraction of dissolved CH4 is oxidized in the water column, which lowers open-water emission per area.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: open-water floodplain lakes < vegetated floodplain habitats (42 vs 118-203 mg CH4 m-2 d-1 in Melack Table 1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Barbosa et al. (2018) found that a large fraction of dissolved CH4 was oxidized with volumetric CH4 oxidation rates ranging from ~1 to 175 mg CH4 m−3 d−1.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The oxidation quote is correct (Sect. 6.1, p. 12, one varzea lake). The Table 1 numbers are correct: open-water lakes 42, floating plants 118, flooded-forest water surface 58, water surface plus stems 203. The source does not attribute the open-water versus vegetated gap to oxidation. Sect. 6.2 (pp. 12-13) instead notes higher CH4 concentrations in herbaceous mats than in open water and lateral export from vegetated habitats. The 203 includes stem flux; the comparable water-surface-only forest value is 58.

crossref.title: Challenges Regionalizing Methane Emissions Using Aquatic Environments in the Amazon Basin as Examples

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Floodplain soil surfaces emit almost nothing once the water table is below the surface, so the non-flooded part of a floodplain contributes near-zero soil flux.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: non-flooded floodplain soil ≈ 0 (±1 mg CH4 m-2 d-1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Soil CH4 fluxes when the water table was below the surface in these plots were low and often negative, ranging from uptake of ~1 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 to evasion of ~1 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 (Gauci et al., 2021).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Sect. 5.3, p. 10: the quote is exact. Soil flux was about +/-1 mg CH4 m-2 d-1 when the water table was below the surface, measured in the Gauci et al. 2021 forested floodplain plots along the Solimoes, Negro and Tapajos rivers.

crossref.title: Challenges Regionalizing Methane Emissions Using Aquatic Environments in the Amazon Basin as Examples

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: The flood pulse supplies substrate: macrophytes that colonize exposed sediments at low water decompose when water rises and boost methanogenesis. Sediment drying and rewetting also increases emissions.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Seasonal floodplains after long low-water periods emit more than they do in steady conditions. This mechanism is specific to the flood pulse.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: during prolonged periods of low water, the growth of macrophytes on exposed sediment, followed by the plant decomposition when water rises, could increase CH4 concentrations and fluxes to the atmosphere
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim in the Conclusion (p.148, right column), and the Abstract makes the same statement ('CH4 emissions were enhanced after a prolonged low water period, when the exposed sediments were colonized by herbaceous plants that decomposed after water levels rose, possibly fueling CH4 production'). Caveats: (a) the paper hedges both mechanisms ('could increase', 'possibly'). The drying-rewetting part comes from the Discussion (p.146), which says drying and rewetting 'could also have contributed', so it should not be stated as fact. (b) The evidence is an interannual contrast at one lake: year 2 (Sep 2015-Sep 2016, after exceptionally low water from Oct to Feb) against year 1. It is not a comparison with 'steady conditions'. (c) 'Specific to the flood pulse' is the extractor's interpretation; the paper does not say it.

crossref.title: Dissolved methane concentrations and fluxes to the atmosphere from a tropical floodplain lake

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Mapped floodplain extent is the leading uncertainty in modelled Amazon floodplain emissions. Vegetation distribution also matters.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Total floodplain emission is modulated by about a factor of 2 through extent alone, and by ~20% through grass versus forest placement.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: uncertainties in floodplain extent (i.e., difference between GLC2000 and PCR-GLOBWB output) modulate the simulated emissions by a factor of about 2 ... Two simulations with the same mean PFT cover, but different spatial distributions of grasslands within the basin, modulated emissions by about 20 %.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The abstract (p.1519) is quoted correctly: extent modulates emissions by a factor of about 2, and grass distribution by about 20 %. Table 7 bears this out: the basin mean is 89.1 without the GLC2000 mask and 44.4 with it. The 20 % is 20.2 % between simulations 1 and 2 (p.1544). 'Leading uncertainty' is the extractor's wording, not a phrase in the paper. It follows from the reported magnitudes, since the other sensitivities are smaller: NPP −11.3 %, depth −3.6 %, IAV +6.6 %, O2 +0.1 %.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from floodplains in the Amazon Basin: challenges in developing a process-based model for global applications

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In the LPX floodplain model, deeper floodwater lowers emissions by increasing oxidation, while a larger flooded area raises them. Lateral inflow of oxygen-rich river water may also lower fluxes in floodplains close to the main channel that flood in many pulses per year.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: deep or frequently flushed floodplain < shallow, stagnant inundated wetland (per area)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: While a flooding depth increase tends to decrease emissions due to increased oxidation, increased floodplain extent leads to increased emissions. ... we recommend first implementing a parameterization that represents higher O2 concentrations for floodplains close to the main channel and characterized by many pulses of flooding per year.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Both quotes are verbatim. The first sentence is on p.1545 but inside Sect. 3.3.2; the paper has no Sect. 3.5. The second is on p.1548, Sect. 4.2, as stated. The depth effect is a qualitative model statement: in the sensitivity runs, the depth change from simulation 1 to 3 gave only −3.6 %, and the O2 effect (Eq. 5) +0.1 %. The oxygen-rich lateral inflow is a hypothesis and a recommendation ('may also play a role'), not a simulated result.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from floodplains in the Amazon Basin: challenges in developing a process-based model for global applications

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Along the Amazon main stem, observed flux densities are higher for floating macrophytes than for flooded forest. Part of the difference may come from different flooding depths.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: within floodplains: herbaceous/macrophyte > flooded forest (surface fluxes)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: In addition, an unknown contribution to this difference may come from differences in flooding depth between these forest and grassland ecosystems.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim, p.1541, Sect. 3.3.2. The same paragraph says the macrophyte-versus-forest difference is not significant around Manaus (Area 2, grass 214.0 vs forest 150.0 ± 98.0), and that the two regions were measured at different times of year.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from floodplains in the Amazon Basin: challenges in developing a process-based model for global applications

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Ebullition carries ~90% of floodplain flux. Seasonally flooded floodplain sites emitted more than permanent lakes.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Pantanal seasonal floodplains > permanent lakes per area. Ebullition dominates in shallow water.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: The bubble flux represented about 90% of the total CH4 losses in the measurements ... The fluxes from lakes were smaller than those observed in the floodplains, where the flooding was more dependent on the seasonal cycle.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Mostly confirmed, with scope corrections. (1) The Abstract says 'The bubble flux represented about 90% of the total CH4 losses in the measurements'. That covers all five sites, lakes included, not the floodplains alone. The discussion on p. 1630 says bubbling 'may account up to more than 90%'. (2) 'The fluxes from lakes were smaller than those observed in the floodplains, where the flooding was more dependent on the seasonal cycle' is printed in the Abstract. Table 1 supports it: floodplain bubble means are 286, 585 and 238 against 148 and 82 for the lakes. (3) 'Ebullition dominates in shallow water' is hedged in the source. The Conclusions say only that shallowness 'could be a decisive factor'. The paper also reports that Medalha Lake, the only site deeper than 2.4 m, had a bubble frequency near that of the shallow floodplains (p. 1631), so no clear depth control was shown.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from lakes and floodplains in Pantanal, Brazil

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Shallow, short flooding and oxic water over sediments make the Orinoco floodplain emit far less than the Amazon. Floodplain soils emit only near standing water when they are very wet.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Deeper, longer flooding with anoxic water gives higher per-area flux (Amazon > Orinoco). Exposed floodplain soils contribute little.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Emission from floodplain soils occurred only when the water content of soil exceeded 25%, which occurred within 20 m of standing water during floodplain drainage (3 months/yr) ... Overall emission rates were notably lower than for the Amazon. The depth and duration of flooding are considerably less for the Orinoco than for the Amazon floodplain; oxygen over sediments is the rule for the Orinoco but not for the Amazon.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote appears word for word in the abstract (p.113). The causal link is stated outright in the Discussion (p.133): 'Differences in methane yield between the Orinoco and Amazon are probably explained by physical differences'. These are deeper water and longer inundation in the Amazon (forest inundated 3.3 months for the Orinoco vs 5.3 for the Amazon), plus anoxia over sediments there. 'Far less' should be quantified with the paper's figure: the Amazon mean areal rate is 'two to three times higher' (p.133). 'Very wet' means soil water content >25%, within 20 m of standing water, during the 3-month drainage phase. Soils contribute ~0% of the total (Table 4: 0.001 Tg).

crossref.title: Methane emissions from the Orinoco River floodplain, Venezuela

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Authors warn that tropical floodplain emissions have been overestimated when inundated area is overestimated.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Per-area and total floodplain emissions may be lower than earlier estimates.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Current information for tropical America, including revised estimates for inundated area along the Amazon, indicate that methane emissions from tropical floodplains have been overestimated.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is the verbatim last sentence of the abstract. The Conclusion (pp.136-137) backs the area argument. SMMR puts the Amazon floodplain water surface at 45,900-46,800 km2, so the areas used by Bartlett et al. (1990) and Devol et al. (1990) are too large. The revised Amazon total is 1-2 Tg yr-1, against the original 2-14. One caveat on the direction field: the Amazon downward revision comes from a smaller area, while per-area rates are kept. 'Lower per-area' applies only to the Orinoco relative to Amazon rates ('grossly overestimated if emission rates per unit area for the Amazon were used'). The paper does not claim that per-area rates in general are lower.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from the Orinoco River floodplain, Venezuela

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Seasonal floodplain emissions collapse when soils dry (oxygenation), whereas the permanent swamp is buffered against drought.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Permanent swamp ~3x seasonal floodplain in a wet year and ~14x in a drought year (122.1 vs 8.7 g m-2); the seasonal-floodplain flux depends on flood extent and duration.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: We conclude that the inter-annual decrease in CH4 emissions at the seasonal floodplain is predominantly attributable to the effect of soil drying, which enables oxygenation of the soil making the edaphic environment less favourable to anaerobic processes such as methanogenesis.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The core claim is confirmed. The quote appears word for word in Sect. 4 Discussion on PDF p. 10 ('We conclude that the inter-annual decrease in CH4 emissions at the seasonal floodplain is predominantly attributable to the effect of soil drying, which enables oxygenation of the soil...'). It is on p. 10, not p. 10–11. The paper also states that 'The 2019 drought had an insignificant effect on the CH4 emissions from the papyrus ecosystem'. Three parts of the 'direction' field are not printed in the source. (1) '~14x' is derived (122.1/8.7 = 14.0); the paper prints only 'factor of three' for 2018 and a floodplain decrease 'by a factor of 4' from 2018 to 2019. (2) Calling 2018 a 'wet year' is loose; the paper says only that 2019 inflow was 40% below 2018 and the lowest on record. (3) The paper names soil water content, from chamber measurements, as the driver. It does not name flood extent or duration as the control of the floodplain CH4 flux.

crossref.title: From sink to source: high inter-annual variability in the carbon budget of a Southern African wetland
crossref.container: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Permanent vegetated (papyrus) swamps emit disproportionately more per unit area than seasonal floodplains in the same delta.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Permanent swamp > seasonal floodplain per area; 24% of area gave 63% (wet year 2018) and 97% (drought 2019) of delta emissions.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: CH4 emissions from the permanent, vegetated wetlands accounted for 63% and 97% of the overall CH4 emission budget for the Okavango Delta during 2018 and 2019, respectively. These wetlands hence play a disproportionate role in the overall budget compared to their source area (24% of total extent).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Quote is printed exactly, on p. 6 in the upscaling subsection of 'Results and discussion'; there is no separate Discussion section. 24% matches Table 1: permanent area is 26% of total extent in 2018 and 21% in 2019. The claim calls 2018 a 'wet year', but the paper does not; it only calls 2019 a drought year with the lowest inflow on record. Better wording: '2018 (normal) and 2019 (drought)'. The 63% and 97% come from upscaling 'using simplified assumptions'. Seasonal budgets are likely overestimated, and the 2018 EC total is more than double the satellite estimate (0.48 vs 0.18 Tg yr-1). The per-area ratio of permanent to seasonal is therefore about 3x in 2018 (117 vs 36 g m-2 yr-1, derived) and about 25x in 2019 (122 vs 4.8, derived).

crossref.title: Phenology is the dominant control of methane emissions in a tropical non-forested wetland

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In a permanent tropical swamp, plant phenology and productivity (GPP of papyrus) control CH4 flux rather than water level.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Permanent swamp flux scales with plant productivity; seasonal floodplain flux scales with water level and temperature until water drops below a threshold.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: phenology is the overarching control of net CH4 emissions to the atmosphere from a permanent, vegetated tropical swamp in the Okavango Delta ... Monthly median fluxes of CH4 (FCH4) measured at the Guma Lagoon papyrus swamp ... are linearly and positively correlated (R2 = 0.89 ...) with monthly maximum gross primary production
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Both quote pieces are printed exactly: the Abstract (p. 1), and p. 2 (R2 = 0.89 with GPPMAX; Fig. 1 gives y = -0.71 + 1.68x, p = 4.7e-06). Two refinements. First, 'rather than water level' for the permanent swamp is an inference: the paper tests GPP, EVI and temperature at Guma, not water level. Second, the floodplain relation to water level is negative, not positive. Fig. 4a gives y = 0.39 - 0.21x (R2 = 0.43, p = 0.055): emissions rose as water level fell. Air temperature was not significant (R2 = 0.06, p = 0.38), and the 2019 drought decoupled flux from both. The text supports 'water level and air temperature are predictors of FCH4, until water levels drop below a critical threshold'. It does not support 'scales with' in the sense of more water giving more flux.

crossref.title: Phenology is the dominant control of methane emissions in a tropical non-forested wetland

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Along a floodplain moisture gradient, emissions peak near 50% soil water content. Rarely flooded (occasional) floodplain soils are net CH4 sinks.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Seasonal floodplain > occasional floodplain, which is a sink; the net sink is ~4% of seasonal-floodplain emission.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Microbial CH4 oxidation of approximately 2.817 × 10−3 ± 0.307 × 10−3 Tg a−1 in adjacent dry soils of the occasional floodplains accounted for the sink of 4% of the total soil CH4 emissions from seasonal floodplains ... The optimum SWC for soil CH4 emissions and oxidation in the Delta were estimated at 50% and 15%, respectively.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed. The abstract quote matches the text, and Sect. 5 and the Conclusion give the same numbers: an occasional-floodplain sink of 2.817e-3 Tg/yr, about 4% of the seasonal-floodplain emission of 0.075 Tg/yr (2.817e-3/0.075 = 3.8%); optimum SWC is 50% for emission and 15% for oxidation. Caveats: (1) SWC is gravimetric on a dry-weight basis (Methods 2d), with values up to about 150%, so '50%' is not volumetric or saturation-fraction water content. Sect. 4 calls the 50% optimum an estimate: 'beyond which SWC appears to suppress' emission. (2) The occasional-floodplain sink is not measured across that zone. It is upscaled from a single fixed dry site (Site 1, 'rarely flooded dry soils'; mean -0.79 +/- 0.09 nmol m-2 s-1) used as a proxy for 54% of the Delta area, and the authors themselves flag this as possibly unrepresentative.

crossref.title: Methane flux measurements along a floodplain soil moisture gradient in the Okavango Delta, Botswana
crossref.container: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Low peat-swamp fluxes come from oxidation in the shallow aerobic peat, lignin-rich substrate in ombrotrophic woody peat, and root O2 supply; floodplain forests on sedimentary soil have higher CH4 production potential.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Floodplain forest on sedimentary (mineral) soil > ombrotrophic tropical peat swamp; the peat swamp is a 'moderate' source despite the hot climate.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: The large difference would be attributable to a higher CH4 production potential of the sedimentary soil in the floodplain forest ... diffusive CH4 efflux from saturated peat is effectively oxidised by bacteria in the shallow aerobic peat layer ... substrate for CH4 production is insufficient in woody peat with much lignin in ombrotrophic conditions ... the oxygen supply through the roots of swamp trees contributes to CH4 oxidation
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: All quoted fragments are printed in Sect. 4.2, but in two different paragraphs. The sentences on oxidation in shallow aerobic peat, lignin-rich woody peat under ombrotrophic conditions, root O2 supply, and 'moderate CH4 source ... despite hot and humid climate' support the peat-swamp part of the claim. The sedimentary-soil sentence is narrower than the claim. It explains why stem CH4 efflux from Amazonian floodplain trees (Pangala et al., 2017) was up to 200 times the stem efflux reported for an Indonesian peat swamp (Pangala et al., 2013). So the source compares tree-stem fluxes, not whole-ecosystem fluxes. It is also Wong's hedged interpretation ('would be attributable'), not a measurement. The direction 'floodplain forest on mineral soil > ombrotrophic peat swamp' should be limited to stem-mediated efflux and cited as secondary.

crossref.title: Micrometeorological measurement of methane flux above a tropical peat swamp forest

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In tropical peat swamps, water table rather than temperature controls flux. The apparent negative temperature correlation comes through its coupling to groundwater level.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Tropical permanent wetlands: the hydrological control dominates and temperature sensitivity is weak.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: In this study, however, FCH4 was negatively correlated with soil temperature despite its narrow seasonal range. This is probably because of the negative correlation of soil temperature with GWL.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is printed verbatim in Sect. 4.1 (Environmental control on CH4 flux). Sect. 3.4 supports the claim: FCH4 shows a concave quadratic relation with GWL, peaking at GWL 0 cm. The negative correlation with soil temperature is attributed to the negative correlation between soil temperature and GWL (r = −0.78). Soil moisture tracks GWL (r = 0.97), and 'these water-related factors are very important in controlling CH4 emissions'. Evidence is one site and 18 months, and soil temperature varied little over the year (annual range within 3.5 °C).

crossref.title: Micrometeorological measurement of methane flux above a tropical peat swamp forest

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Standing water and nutrient-rich substrates keep shallow pore water CH4-rich; tree stems then vent it past the methanotroph layer.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Nutrient-rich flooded wetlands (e.g. Amazon floodplains) > nutrient-poor peat; flux is higher when standing water is present; the tree pathway adds to per-area flux in forested wetlands.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: more nutrient-rich tropical wetlands typically contain higher concentrations of CH4 in shallow pore water ... High concentrations of CH4 in shallow soil are particularly common where standing water is present, because it impedes entry of O2 to support methanotrophy
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Quote is verbatim on p. 529 (Results and Discussion; the paper has no separate Discussion). Three caveats. (1) The quote is about CH4 concentration in shallow pore water, not flux. (2) 'Nutrient-rich > SE Asian peat' is cited from Wassmann et al. 1992, not measured in this study: 'Tropical peat forests in Southeast Asia are known to emit less CH4 than nutrient-rich tropical wetlands', p. 528. (3) Higher flux with standing water is supported in-study by ponded hollows (32.9 ± 7.8 ug m-2 h-1) vs hummocks (0.7 ± 0.5 ug m-2 h-1), p. 527. The bypass of methanotrophs by trees is stated in the Introduction (p. 525). The paper also says the actual tree contribution in other tropical forested wetlands 'remains unknown' (p. 529). So 'tree pathway adds to per-area flux' is shown for this site and only suggested as potential elsewhere.

crossref.title: Trees are major conduits for methane egress from tropical forested wetlands
crossref.vol_pages: 197(2): 524-531 (published-print 2013-01; Crossref 'issued'/online 2012-12-18; authors Pangala, Moore, Hornibrook, Gauci)

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In tropical peat swamp forest, much of the CH4 produced in the peat is oxidized at the oxic-anoxic interface before reaching the peat surface, so surface fluxes are low. Trees provide a bypass.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: tropical peat swamp surface flux low (1-3 mg m-2 d-1 ecosystem total in wet season)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Although significant quantities of CH4 are produced in the peat, CH4 typically is not released at high rates from the peat surface to the atmosphere because methanotrophic bacteria oxidize CH4 at the oxic–anoxic interface in soil and within the rhizosphere
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Introduction, p. 525. It is a general statement citing Couwenberg et al. 2010, not a result of this study. 'Trees provide a bypass' is supported: 'enabling methane to bypass soil methanotrophs' (p. 525). The direction field mixes two quantities. 1-3 mg m-2 d-1 (derived 1.08-3.28) is the ecosystem total including trees, which make up 62-87% of it; it is not the peat-surface flux. The surface-only flux per plot area is about 4.0 g ha-1 d-1 ≈ 0.40 mg m-2 d-1 (hollows 3.9 g ha-1 d-1 + hummocks about 0.08). These are wet-season values only.

crossref.title: Trees are major conduits for methane egress from tropical forested wetlands
crossref.vol_pages: 197(2): 524-531 (published-print 2013-01; Crossref 'issued'/online 2012-12-18; authors Pangala, Moore, Hornibrook, Gauci)

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In the Pantanal, emissions pulse just after water starts rising and decline before maximum water level. Prognostic wetland models get the magnitude right but the phase wrong.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Seasonal floodplain: highest per-area flux in the rising-water phase, not at maximum inundated area.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: CH4 being released in large amounts just after water levels begin to rise again after minimum levels have been reached. CH4 emissions decline substantially once the maximum water level has been reached. While predictions with prognostic wetland CH4 emission models agree well with the magnitude of the fluxes, they disagree with the phasing.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quoted text matches the Crossref abstract word for word, and the first author and year match (Gloor, 2021). The full text I checked is the White Rose accepted manuscript (eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/179703/6/2021GB006964.pdf); the local gloor2021.pdf is truncated and gloor2021b.pdf is an HTML error page. One wording problem: the abstract says emissions decline 'once the maximum water level has been reached', not before it. The 'before maximum' version is in the Discussion on p. 9: 'Emissions start to decrease before maximum flood levels have been reached' and 'maximum emissions precede maximum inundated area'. So the claim should cite p. 9, not the abstract. The Key Points back the stated direction: 'CH4 flux is large during the early expansion phase of the inundated area and weakens at peak extent'. The per-area basis holds by construction. The authors assume the PBL-budget flux (0 to 0.4 g CH4 m-2 d-1) is spread evenly over the flooded area and multiply it by monthly GIEMS flooded area to get 2.0-2.8 Tg CH4/yr (p. 8). This flux is an atmospheric (boundary-layer) estimate, not a chamber measurement. The mechanism is described in the paper as unclear. The authors suggest two causes: fresh organic substrate carried in by rising water, and low hydrostatic pressure early in the rise. The model part is also confirmed (p. 10). LPJ-wsl and JULES peak fluxes are similar in magnitude to the observations, and LPJ-wsl gives 2.2 Tg/yr for Sep 2017-Aug 2018. LPJ-wsl flux follows water level with no lag, so it misses the observed phase shift of several months. Caveats: the record is short (Mar 2017 to Sep 2019), and GOSAT column data add support. The inversion total is about 3.3 Tg/yr in the abstract but 3.5 Tg/yr in the body; this does not affect the claim.

crossref.title: Large Methane Emissions From the Pantanal During Rising Water-Levels Revealed by Regularly Measured Lower Troposphere CH4 Profiles

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Flood depth matters: the largest wetland CH4 emissions come from water deeper than 40 cm (from Zou et al. 2022 as cited).
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Deeper standing water gives higher per-area flux. Shallow, receding water favours CO2 instead.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Wetland methane emissions increase with both spatial extent and flood depth, with the largest emissions coming from waters deeper than 40 cm, whereas CO2 emissions peak as water table levels recede to below ground surface level (Zou et al. 2022).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote appears word for word in Sect. 2.3 'Swamp Forest GHG Emissions'. This was checked in the local PMC full text (PMC12895296, scratchpad perarea/congo2026.txt, character offset about 13423). Sect. 4.3 says the same thing again: 'deeper waters emitting larger quantities of CH4 and shallower WTLs emitting increased CO2 in tropical wetlands (Zou et al. 2022)'. Crossref lists the authors as Byrne, Williams and Pettorelli, with the year 2026, which matches the claim. Caveats: (1) This is a secondary citation. Byrne et al. took the 40 cm class and the depth dependence from the WTL aggregation of Zou et al. 2022 (Nature Geoscience 15(8):627-632, doi 10.1038/s41561-022-00989-0, Table S3) and did not measure them. The primary source should be cited for the threshold. (2) Sect. 2.3 says only that 'emissions increase with both spatial extent and flood depth'. The source does not state the per-area reading outright. It is implied because depth is listed separately from extent, and Sect. 4.3 says the same for tropical wetlands. Derived context, not printed as a per-area value: the Congo swamp-forest CH4 is 13.57 (8.02-19.12) Mt in 2007 and 14.96 (8.88-21.04) Mt in 2024. Dividing by the swamp-forest extent (195,345 and 222,467 km2) gives about 69 and 67 g CH4 m-2 yr-1. The emission total may also include non-flooded pixels with a below-ground WTL inside the maximum flood extent, so this area basis is uncertain.

crossref.title: Wetland Expansion Reduces CO2-Equivalent Emissions and Strengthens the Congo Basin's Role as a Net Carbon Sink

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Model calibration needed a ~5x higher methanogenesis base rate at a tropical site than at boreal or temperate sites, with a low Q10.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Tropical wetlands have higher per-area production potential. Temperature sensitivity is weak in the tropics.
confirmed_mechanisms.location_in_source: Sect. on parameter optimization, paragraphs [11]-[12], p. 4
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: At the tropical (Panama) site, the optimized Q10 is found to be only of 1.48 ± 0.56 ... Contrary to Q10, the optimized value of a0 is larger for the tropical site than for the other sites (by a factor of ∼5).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is word for word, with an ellipsis: the Q10 sentence is para [11] and the a0 sentence is para [12], both on p. 4 in Sect. 2.3 'Site-Level Model Optimization'. The factor of about 5 holds: Table 1 optimal a0 is Abisko 2.63, Michigan 2.45, Panama 13.75 (x10^-6 m-1 month-1), ratios 5.2–5.6; the means 2.80, 2.44 and 13.61 give ratios of about 4.9–5.6. The value 1.48 ± 0.56 is the MEAN Q10 over the tested pairs; the optimal Panama Q10 is 1.20. The claim sentence itself is supported. The direction field goes further than the source: the paper says the low Q10 'results from the anticorrelation between temperature and flux density at this specific site'. It warns that 'we are looking at only one site that may not be representative of the whole tropics'. For that reason it also tests a tropical pair with Q10 = 3.2. So 'temperature sensitivity is weak in the tropics' should not be stated as a general finding. 'Higher per-area production potential' also needs a qualifier: a0 multiplies ORCHIDEE labile carbon, and the authors say the gap may partly come from ORCHIDEE's simple soil-carbon pools (para [12]).

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: The optimized base methanogenesis rate a0 at the tropical (Panama) site is about 5 times that at the boreal and temperate sites, which the authors attribute to substrate amount and quality. The 2011 ORCHIDEE-WET optimization gives a0 = 3.51, 2.63 and 15.77 x10^-6 m-1 month-1 for Abisko, Michigan and Panama.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: tropical > boreal/temperate (per area, via substrate)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Contrary to Q10, the optimized value of a0 is larger for the tropical site than for the other sites (by a factor of ∼5). This order of magnitude between the tropical site and the others concerning the amount and the quality of substrate is consistent with what Walter and Heimann [2000] also discussed for R0.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The 2010 part is confirmed: para [12], p. 4 states 'by a factor of ∼5', and the quoted sentence about the amount and quality of substrate, consistent with Walter and Heimann [2000] for R0, is word for word. The attribution is only partial. The next sentence gives a second explanation: 'The larger discrepancy between sites at different latitudes may also result from the very weak number of carbon soils pools in ORCHIDEE (e.g., not accounting for the exudates pool) and the simple way in which carbon dynamics is computed.' The 2011 values 3.51, 2.63 and 15.77 x10^-6 m-1 month-1 (Abisko, Michigan, Panama) are word for word in Ringeval et al. 2011, Biogeosciences 8, 2137–2157, p. 2154 (checked in the local text 2011_Ringeval_ORCHIDEE_climate_ch4_feedback.txt, lines 1064–1066). That is a DIFFERENT DOI (10.5194/bg-8-2137-2011), so these values must not be cited to 10.1029/2008GB003354. The 2011 run re-optimized a0 because ORCHIDEE was run with water stress, which changed the carbon stocks; the Panama ratio there is 4.5–6.0. Do not mix these values with the 2010 Table 1 values (2.63, 2.45, 13.75). Note that 2.63 is Abisko in 2010 but Michigan in 2011.
