confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In Kalimantan peat swamp forests, CH4 efflux is negligible in the carbon balance.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: Permanent tropical peat swamp: low per-area CH4.
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: However, methane efflux was negligibly small in the carbon balance of tropical peatlands in this area (Hirano et al., 2009; Page et al., 2009).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim, but the page is wrong. It sits in the Discussion on p. 3420, not p. 3419 (pdftotext of docs/refs/sites/ID-Pag/2012_Hirano.pdf: the PDF page headed 3420 has 'Discussion' at line 22 and the quote at line 49). A near-identical sentence is also in the Introduction on p. 3411: 'methane efflux was reported to be negligibly small in the carbon balance of tropical peat swamp forests (Hirano et al., 2009; Page et al., 2009)'. Caveats on how this should be used: (1) This paper did not measure CH4. The statement is second-hand, citing Hirano et al. 2009 and Page et al. 2009, and gives no CH4 flux number, so it cannot supply a per-area value. (2) 'Negligible in the carbon balance' is about carbon mass: CH4-C is small next to NEE of about 100-600 gC m-2 yr-1. That does not show that per-area CH4 is low in absolute terms. (3) The label 'Permanent tropical peat swamp' does not fit these sites. They are partly drained Kalimantan peat forests: UF has a canal network and was selectively logged, and DF is drained. Groundwater stays below the surface: at the DF site the annual-mean GWL is about -0.53 m (Table 1, p. 3414), and monthly means run from -0.24 m in April to -0.99 m in October (p. 3415). The minus signs are lost in the text conversion but are clear from context. So the claim supports 'CH4 is a small carbon term in drained or seasonally unsaturated tropical peat swamp forest', not low CH4 per area in a permanently inundated swamp.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In created riparian marshes with Midwestern-floodplain-like hydrology, intermittently flooded zones emitted about 30% of permanently inundated zones. Macrophytes made no difference in intermittent zones.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: permanent > intermittent by about 3.3x (annual); growing season about 8 vs 3.5 mg CH4-C m-2 h-1
confirmed_mechanisms.location_in_source: Abstract (via web search index; publisher page 403)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Average growing season rates of methane flux from intermittently flooded zones with and without macrophytes did not differ significantly (∼3.5mg CH4–C m−2h−1), but both were significantly less than those from permanently inundated areas (∼8mg CH4–C m−2h−1).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote matches the abstract word for word: '~3.5 mg CH4-C m-2 h-1' for intermittent zones with and without macrophytes versus '~8 mg CH4-C m-2 h-1' for permanently inundated areas, and the 30% annual ratio. The direction permanent > intermittent (1/0.30 = about 3.3x annual; 8/3.5 = about 2.3x growing season) is correct. One caveat: the 'no macrophyte effect' is only a statement that growing-season average rates showed no significant difference. The abstract says nothing about a macrophyte effect on annual totals.

crossref.title: Methane flux from created riparian marshes: Relationship to intermittent versus continuous inundation and emergent macrophytes

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Pulsing hydrology in riverine wetlands slowed CH4 emissions.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: steady inundation > pulsed
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Pulsing hydrology, which is common in these riverine wetlands, was shown to slow down the methane emissions in certain parts of these wetlands as well in a comparison in 2004 and 2005 (Altor and Mitsch 2008).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim on p. 248. The next sentence reads 'Higher methane emissions under steady-flow hydrology have also been reported in several rice paddy studies', so the direction steady > pulsed matches the source's wording. Caveats: (1) The effect is stated for 'certain parts of these wetlands' and is cited from Altor and Mitsch 2008, not new data. (2) The whole-wetland annual values in Table 4 show no such difference: 2004 pulsing vs 2005 steady flow is 16 vs 16 (planted) and 32 vs 31 (unplanted) g C m-2 yr-1. (3) 'Steady' means steady pumped inflow with flood pulses suppressed (Table 3 header 'Flood pulses suppressed (2005)'). It does not mean steady inundation, so 'steady inundation > pulsed' slightly over-reads the source.

crossref.title: Creating Wetlands: Primary Succession, Water Quality Changes, and Self-Design over 15 Years

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In a temperate floodplain swamp, significant CH4 flux occurred only at flooded sites and was concentrated in the most frequently inundated area. About half of the CH4 entering floodwater was oxidized in the water column, and emission shut off below about 15 °C soil temperature.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: frequently inundated low habitats >> rarely flooded floodplain; water-column oxidation and cold-season floods reduce per-area flux
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Over 90% of the total floodplain CH4 emissions came from the 30% of the floodplain that was most frequently inundated. [...] Roughly half of the CH4 that entered the water column was consumed without reaching the atmosphere. [...] No significant CH4 emissions occurred when soil temperatures were below 15°C
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed. All three quoted sentences appear word for word in the Crossref abstract: 'Significant atmospheric CH4 fluxes were found only at flooded sites'; 'Over 90% of the total floodplain CH4 emissions came from the 30% of the floodplain that was most frequently inundated'; 'Roughly half of the CH4 that entered the water column was consumed without reaching the atmosphere' (the abstract ties this to oxidation measured by in situ bottle incubations); and 'No significant CH4 emissions occurred when soil temperatures were below 15°C'. The abstract calls the temperature effect a step function: above 15°C, rates show no further link to temperature. That supports the 'shut off below ~15 °C' wording. The clause in the direction field that 'cold-season floods reduce per-area flux' is a fair inference but is not stated directly.

crossref.title: Carbon Dioxide and Methane Exports from a Southeastern Floodplain Swamp

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Floodplain swamp CH4 is controlled by river discharge (inundation), and hydrology matters more than direct temperature effects.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: more river discharge (longer or larger flooding) gives higher emission; a 20% rainfall decrease gives 30–43% lower emission
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: with a 20% decrease in rainfall resulting in 30–43% declines in methane emissions. [...] hydrologic impacts of changes in evapotranspiration rates (such as may occur in response to temperature shifts) were more important than direct temperature effects on methane production.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Both quoted passages appear word for word in the abstract (p.151), which also says emissions 'responded very strongly to changes in river discharge'. The body (p.167) confirms the direction: a 20% drop in precipitation gave 30% lower emission in the TI model and 43% in the TD model, and a 20% rise gave 22-24% higher. Caveat: this is a model result. Temperature enters the model only as a 15.5 C step, and flux is I x R, so the finding that hydrology dominates is partly built into the model structure. The paper also says the TI model predicts higher emission under warming at all precipitation levels, and that the sign of the temperature effect depends on how evapotranspiration (ET) is represented.

crossref.title: Methane emissions from floodplain swamps of the Ogeechee River: long-term patterns and effects of climate change
crossref.vol_pages: 15(3); Crossref gives no page field. Springer citation metadata and the PDF header give pp. 151-174. Authors: Pulliam WM, Meyer JL. Author and year match the claims.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In a paired temperate marsh comparison, the permanently inundated marsh emitted about 9x more per area than the seasonally inundated marsh, and the shrub swamp emitted nearly zero.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: permanent (39.40 g C) >> seasonal (4.36 g C) >> shrub swamp (0.21 g C m-2 yr-1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: the mean annual budgets of CH4 [...] were 39.40 ± 6.99 g C m−2 yr−1 [...] for permanently inundated wetland; 4.36 ± 1.79 g C m−2 yr−1 [...] for seasonally inundated wetland
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed by the abstract: 39.40/4.36 = 9.0x per area, and the shrub swamp emits 0.21 g C m−2 yr−1, which is near zero. Three caveats. First, the abstract says 'three wetland ecosystems' and 'wetland'; 'marsh' is the extractor's label. Second, the seasonal value is averaged over the whole wetland area and the whole year, not per flooded area, so the 9x ratio mixes a hydroperiod effect with a per-flooded-area rate difference. Third, the paper attributes the differences among the three types to wetland type in general and does not isolate inundation duration as the cause.

crossref.title: Ecosystem–atmosphere exchange of CH4 and N2O and ecosystem respiration in wetlands in the Sanjiang Plain, Northeastern China

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: After rewetting of a river-valley fen, the permanently inundated site emitted about 28x the non-inundated site. The high emissions are attributed to fresh litter from plant die-back, and they ended once Typha colonized.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: inundated >> non-inundated; new flooding of vegetated land adds labile litter substrate
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: The increased annual CH4 emissions at our inundated measurement site during the first years after rewetting might be due to the high input of fresh plant litter through initial plant die-back.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim, but it sits in Sect. 4.4 on p. 3687, not on pp. 3683-3685. The Typha decline is discussed on pp. 3687-3688. The quote is hedged ('might be due to'). The title and Sect. 4.4 support the Typha claim: 'The strong decline in annual CH4 emissions in the last 2 years of the study (2016 and 2017) coincides with the establishment of helophytes, mainly T. latifolia'. The '28x' is not printed in the paper. It is derived as 83.9/3.0 = 28.0, and the two means cover unequal periods (14 yr vs 12 yr). Over the common 2004-2015 period the ratio is 94.6/3.0 = 31.5. The attribution is incomplete. Sect. 4.4 names three carbon sources: initial plant die-back; litter of newly established aquatic plants (Ceratophyllum, Lemnaceae), which 'have apparently been potent C sources for the very high CH4 emissions'; and lateral C transfer from the surrounding helophyte belt, 'the third major C source'. So the high emissions are not attributed to die-back litter alone. The paper lists four processes for the decline: lower substrate, higher oxidation in the rooted layer, microclimate cooling and reduced lateral input.

crossref.title: The unexpected long period of elevated CH4 emissions from an inundated fen meadow ended only with the occurrence of cattail (Typha latifolia)

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Eutrophic conditions combined with permanent high inundation give very high CH4 in rewetted fens. Open water emitted 4x more than emergent stands.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: permanently inundated eutrophic open water > vegetated
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: We assume the eutrophic conditions in combination with permanent high inundation as major reasons for the unfavourable GHG balance.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim from the abstract, p. 3051: 'We assume the eutrophic conditions in combination with permanent high inundation as major reasons for the unfavourable GHG balance.' The abstract also says the global warming impact was 'mainly driven by high CH4 emissions'. It states that open-water CH4 emissions were 'around 4-fold higher than from emergent vegetation stands', and the results section says 'more than 4-fold'. One nuance: the stated cause is given for the unfavourable GHG balance, which includes high CO2 release, not for CH4 alone. The paper also names unusual weather, a warm dry summer and a mild winter, as a possible driver of high respiration.

crossref.title: High net CO2 and CH4 release at a eutrophic shallow lake on a formerly drained fen

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Transiently flooded (under 2 months per year) subtropical pastures were net GHG sources from CH4. Short floods on non-wetland soil can emit substantially.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: brief warm-season flooding of productive grassland can yield large CH4
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Even transiently flooded subtropical pastures were GHG sources due to large CH4 fluxes, despite being inundated for less than 2 months of the year (Chamberlain et al., 2016; Chamberlain, Groffman, et al., 2017).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim, but it is on p. 6085, not p. 6084. It is a secondary citation: Hemes cites Chamberlain et al. (2016) and Chamberlain, Groffman et al. (2017) and reports no pasture flux value of its own. The source supports this part only: a subtropical pasture inundated for less than 2 months per year was a net GHG source because of large CH4 fluxes. The source does not say three things in the extracted claim: (a) 'warm-season' flooding, (b) the generalisation that short floods on non-wetland soil can emit substantially, and (c) 'productive grassland'. These are the extractor's interpretation. For any per-area number, cite Chamberlain et al. directly. The sweep label 'temperate' does not fit a subtropical pasture.

crossref.title: A Biogeochemical Compromise: The High Methane Cost of Sequestering Carbon in Restored Wetlands

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Raised surface water (beaver ponds) raised the adjacent bog water table and CH4.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: higher water level gives higher CH4 in a bog
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Raised water level in the beaver ponds led to higher water tables and increased CH4 emission in the peatland.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote 'Raised water level in the beaver ponds led to higher water tables and increased CH4 emission in the peatland.' is word for word in the abstract. The claim matches the quote, and the direction (a higher water table gives more CH4 in the bog) is supported. The Discussion gives the size of the effect. Beavers were removed in 1998-2000 and came back around 2005. The mean May-Oct water table rose from -46 cm (1998-2003) to -39 cm (2004-2008), and the Conclusions say peripheral beaver dams 'can profoundly affect CH4 fluxes'. One caveat: the estimated annual CH4 flux for 2004-05 to 2008-09 was NOT significantly correlated with the mean May-Oct water table (r2 = 0.32, P = 0.32, n = 5). The authors say the frequency distribution and timing of the water table matter too, not just its mean. The effect is interannual and applies to the peatland next to the ponds. It is not a flux from the ponds themselves.

crossref.title: A Multi-Year Record of Methane Flux at the Mer Bleue Bog, Southern Canada

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Seasonally inundated temperate floodplain meadows are net but small CH4 sources. Emissions depend on high water table and aerenchymatous plants, and oxic-period uptake partly offsets them.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: floodplain meadow (1.14 g) << IPCC temperate wetland EF (23.5 g CH4 m-2 yr-1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Mean annual flux was 1.14 g CH4 m−2 year−1 for all vegetated mesocosms, and for the field modelling, which is considerably lower than the IPCC (2014) emission factor of 23.5 g CH4 m−2 year−1 for temperate inland wetlands on mineral soils.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim in Sect. 4.5 'Implications': 'Mean annual flux was 1.14 g CH4 m-2 year-1 for all vegetated mesocosms, and for the field modelling, which is considerably lower than the IPCC (2014) emission factor of 23.5 g CH4 m-2 year-1 for temperate inland wetlands on mineral soils.' The 1.14 << 23.5 direction is confirmed. The drivers are also confirmed: high water table plus aerenchymatous plants (abstract and highlights: 'driven by high water tables and plant species with arenchymatous tissue'), and oxic-period uptake outweighed by flooding-induced anoxic emissions (abstract). One qualifier: the abstract says floodplain meadows 'can be either small sources or sinks of CH4 over an annual cycle', and A. pratensis mesocosms at 45 cm WT were net sinks. 'Net but small sources' holds for the field upscaling at Cricklade North Meadow, not for every condition.

crossref.title: Water table depth and plant species determine the direction and magnitude of methane fluxes in floodplain meadow soils

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In a short-hydroperiod floodplain, CH4 flux is near zero and set by O2 availability, not by C inputs from flood sedimentation or vegetation.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: short-hydroperiod floodplain soil ≈ 0; wettest geomorphic unit (backswamp) highest
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Spatial variation in aerobic and anaerobic respiration was thus controlled by oxygen availability but was not related to C inputs from sedimentation or vegetation.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote matches the abstract word for word. One caveat: the source sentence is about spatial variation in 'aerobic and anaerobic respiration' in general (CO2 and CH4 together). The link to CH4 comes from the sentence before it ('annual CH4 emissions had the opposite pattern of CO2', i.e., CH4 rises with soil water-filled pore space). The abstract does not say that the near-zero magnitude itself is 'set by' O2. Suggested wording: 'spatial variation in CH4 (highest in the wettest unit, the backswamp) tracks O2 availability and not C inputs from sedimentation or vegetation; fluxes are near zero overall.' The direction field ('≈ 0; backswamp highest') is consistent with the abstract.

crossref.title: Soil greenhouse gas emissions and carbon budgeting in a short-hydroperiod floodplain wetland

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In seasonally inundated forested wetlands, inundation extent and duration (not frequency or depth) drive CH4, and intermittently inundated soils switch between source and sink. Accounting for variable inundated area gives 57–74% of fixed-area estimates.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: emission scales with inundated area x duration; flux is higher when water levels are falling
confirmed_mechanisms.location_in_source: Abstract; Results (IOP page via web fetch)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Our results show that inundation extent and duration, but not frequency or depth, were major drivers of wetland methane emissions. [...] Intermittently inundated soils alternated between being sources and sinks of methane depending on water level, soil moisture, and the direction of water level change.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The published abstract, read verbatim from Crossref and DOAJ, contains both quoted sentences: 'inundation extent and duration, but not frequency or depth, were major drivers of wetland methane emissions' and 'Intermittently inundated soils alternated between being sources and sinks of methane depending on water level, soil moisture, and the direction of water level change.' It also states that 'emissions were generally higher when water levels were falling.' The figure 57–74% was confirmed in the dissertation Chapter 1 Results (line 1251): 'Emissions estimated using variable inundation extents were between 57–74% of the emissions calculated under the fixed-area model.' This could not be checked against the publisher PDF because of the captcha. The Discussion says the same thing another way: areal rates are 26–43% lower, a scaling factor of about 64% of wetland area is suggested, and inundated zones gave 83–99% of emissions. Caveat: all wetland-scale estimates are for diffusive flux only.

crossref.title: Effects of seasonal inundation on methane fluxes from forested freshwater wetlands

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Timing of floodplain flooding controls emission. Autumn/winter floods give negligible CH4, while summer floods start emission within 3–6 days. At peak, ephemeral floodplain wetlands equal permanent wetlands per area, and methanogens survive long drying.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: per flooded area at peak: ephemeral ≈ permanent; cold-season flooding << warm-season flooding
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: emissions from these sites were usually negligible after flooding in autumn or winter. In contrast, the onset of methane emission was very rapid (within 3 to 6 days) after the depressions had been flooded in summer [...] At their peak, emissions from the ephemeral wetlands were similar to peak emissions from permanent wetlands in south-eastern Australia.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The abstract text matches the quoted sentences word for word. The paper's wording is softer than the claim in three places. It says 'usually negligible', not always negligible, after autumn/winter flooding, and this applies to the three small depressions (Murray, Kiewa). It says 'similar to', not equal to, peak emissions from permanent SE Australian wetlands. The 3-6 day onset applies to summer-flooded depressions. Two findings qualify the claim. First, the replicated mesocosms were 'always very small (<0.2 mmol m-2 h-1), regardless of time of flooding, water depths, or season', so flooding timing did not control emission there. Second, in vitro incubations showed 'a progressive decrease in benthic methanogenesis with sediment desiccation'. The paper does support 'survival and rapid reactivation of methanogenic archaea after prolonged drying', but survival comes with reduced potential, not unchanged activity. The peak-to-peak comparison with permanent wetlands is qualitative in the abstract; no permanent-wetland number is given there.

crossref.title: Effects of wetting and drying on methane emissions from ephemeral floodplain wetlands in south-eastern Australia

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In the Danube floodplain, isolated floodplain waters have higher CH4 concentrations and fluxes than connected ones. During surface connection, CH4 is exported to the river ('exhaust pipe'). The 100-yr flood year emitted 34% more.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: isolated > connected floodplain waters; floods flush stored CH4 laterally
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Hydrologically isolated habitats in general have higher concentrations and produce higher fluxes despite lower physically defined velocities. During surface connection, however, CH4 is exported from the floodplain to the river, suggesting that the main channel serves as an 'exhaust pipe' for the floodplain.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote matches the abstract verbatim, including the 'exhaust pipe' wording. The abstract also states '34% more CH4 was emitted from the entire system during the year with the 100-yr flood compared to a hydrologically "normal" year', and Results confirm it: '34% more CH4 (kmol yr−1)', Fig. 7. Two caveats: isolated > connected refers to open-water diffusive evasion per unit water area, and the 34% is a system-wide total that includes the expanded flooded area (Table 3), not a per-area increase.

crossref.title: Aquatic methane dynamics in a human-impacted river-floodplain of the Danube
crossref.vol_pages: 61(S1); Crossref gives no page or article number; the PMC JATS copy (PMC5117262) gives fpage S175, lpage S187. Published online 2016-06-20, issue 2016-11.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Floodplain lakes: lentic (isolated) oxbows emit about 24x more per water area than lotic (connected) ones.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: isolated > connected (507 vs 21 mg m-2 d-1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Average CH4 fluxes from the lakes were 21, 225 and 507 mg m-2 day-1 for lotic, semi-lotic and lentic systems, respectively
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed. The abstract and Table 2 support the direction: isolated (lentic) > semi-lotic > connected (lotic). The difference between lentic and lotic is significant (one-way ANOVA with Duncan post hoc test, p ≤ 0.05; Table 2 superscripts a/b/c). The ratio is 24.1× with the abstract's rounded values (507/21) and 23.4× with Table 2 (506.91/21.68), so 'about 24×' is acceptable, and '~23–24×' is more exact. Limits: the result is per open-water area of oxbow lakes from midday floating-chamber snapshots at one temperate river. It says nothing about per-area emissions from vegetated floodplain soils or permanent wetlands. The paper attributes the gradient to low oxygen, organic and macrophyte build-up and methanogen dominance (low MOB/mGen) in isolated lakes. It gives river connectivity as the driver, not flooding frequency.

crossref.title: Microbial Communities Drive Methane Fluxes From Floodplain Lakes—A Hydrological Gradient Perspective

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: On a seasonally flooded lake floodplain, CH4 is tiny during drying and very large at drying–wetting transitions.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: rewetting transitions >> dry phase (8219 vs 36 μg m-2 h-1)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: The mean ecosystem CH4 emission rate was 36 μg CH4 m−2 h−1 for drying periods, but 8219 μg CH4 m−2 h−1 for drying-wetting transition periods.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim (Abstract and Results) and supports the direction claimed: transition 8219 >> drying 36 μg CH4 m−2 h−1. Discussion adds that drying-period fluxes were low because there was no standing water and soil moisture was relatively low (water table −30 to −50 cm). For floodplain per-area reasoning, the largest contribution is not the transition pulses. It is the inundated summer period, 18 of the 21 g CH4 m−2 in 2010 (86%, Table 2). The transition pulses rest on few sampling dates.

crossref.title: Plant-mediated methane and nitrous oxide fluxes from a carex meadow in Poyang Lake during drawdown periods

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Standing-water depth controls marsh CH4 by setting how much plant litter is inundated (labile C for methanogens). Stem density controls transport.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: deeper and longer standing water gives higher CH4 (within marsh range)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Both the flux rates and spatial variation of CH(4) emissions strongly increased as standing water depth increased significantly. Standing water depth greatly governed the spatial variation of CH(4) emissions from different marshes in a region by changing the amount of plant litters inundated in standing water, which provided labile organic C for methanogens
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote matches the abstract word for word. Among marshes, standing-water depth governs spatial variation by changing how much plant litter is inundated, which supplies labile organic C to methanogens and controls porewater CH4. Within one marsh, the abstract credits aboveground plant biomass, which works through the emission pathways (stem density). So 'stem density controls transport' is supported only at the within-marsh scale. The direction field adds 'and longer': duration of standing water appears nowhere in the abstract, which states only that fluxes and their variation 'strongly increased as standing water depth increased'. Supported direction: deeper standing water gives higher CH4.

In the older W1 scenario, 'typical' peat-rich bogs were also assigned 0.2 g CH4/m2/d (p. 13,039), which ties with alluvial formations. confirmed_mechanisms.direction: steady inundation > pulsed inundation (2x in deep zones); edge zones have a shorter emission season

confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The Crossref author (Altor, Mitsch) and year (2008) match the claim. Only the abstract was opened (Springer landing page, saved to scratchpad/perarea/altor2008_springer.html). The full text is paywalled (isAccessibleForFree=false), so no table was checked. The quote is verbatim from the abstract, and the [...] leaves out one sentence on emergent vegetation. Three corrections to the paraphrase. (1) The abstract says edge-zone CH4 fluxes were 'only substantial in spring and summer', not that edge zones emitted 'only' in those seasons. Reword to 'edge-zone fluxes were substantial only in spring and summer'. (2) 'Twice as high' compares two years (2004-2005) in two created, managed river-fed experimental marshes at the Olentangy River Wetland Research Park in Ohio, USA, with hydrology manipulated to simulate pulse versus steady flow. Treatment and year are confounded, and this is an artificial pulse regime, not natural floodplain inundation. 'Halved by pulsing' should be phrased as 'about 2x higher in continuously inundated zones in the steady-flow year than in the pulsed year'. (3) The abstract adds that edge-zone fluxes did not differ significantly between years, and that the hydrology effect was 'only in the deeper areas of the wetlands'. confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Hydrological fluctuation regenerates alternative electron acceptors (Fe, Mn, SO4, humics), which inhibits and delays methanogenesis after re-inundation. CH4 lags water-table changes by weeks.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: fluctuating (seasonal) < steadily wet, per area; drought-to-inundation transitions reported 5-fold lower than steady wet conditions
confirmed_mechanisms.location_in_source: Sections 'Alternative electron acceptors' and 'Uncertainty of methane fluxes under hydrological fluctuations'
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: hydrological fluctuations can induce the repeated renewal of alternative electron acceptor pools, enabling alternative electron acceptors to re-engage in anaerobic respiration processes during post-drought inundation. This dynamic process inhibits and delays CH4 production [...] seasonal CH4 flux changes could lag water table fluctuations by about 17 ± 11 days across 23 wetland sites [...] a 5-fold lower CH4 emission during the transition from drought to inundation compared to the steady wet conditions
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quotes are verbatim, but they come from two different sections. 'repeated renewal ... inhibits and delays CH4 production' is in 'Alternative electron acceptors' (under 'Effects of hydrological fluctuations on methane production', citing refs 176-178, Knorr & Blodau 2009 and Peiffer 2021). The source hedges it as 'potentially explaining the lagged response'. The same paragraph says prolonged inundation (e.g., 50 days) largely depletes the acceptors. The acceptors it names are iron, manganese, sulfate and organic acceptors; it does not say 'humics' there. The '17 ± 11 days across 23 wetland sites' (ref 24, Knox 2021 GCB) and the '5-fold lower' (ref 126, Tangen & Bansal 2019) are in 'Uncertainty of methane fluxes under hydrological fluctuations'. The 'direction' field goes too far. The 5-fold is a SHORT-TERM lag effect 'during the transition from drought to inundation compared to the steady wet conditions'. It is not an annual or per-area comparison between fluctuating and permanently wet wetlands, so it should not be used as a per-area class ratio. The source also gives lags ranging from a few days to a few months, and up to eight months in tropical wetlands (ref 125), not only 'weeks'.

confirmed_mechanisms.direction: permanently flooded soil has lower oxidation, so higher net emission than pulsating soil
confirmed_mechanisms.location_in_source: Section 'Effects of hydrological fluctuations on methane oxidation'
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: This region is often located close to the water table fluctuation zone (e.g., the mesotelm in peatlands), implying that pulsating soils with CH4 oxidation hotspots possess higher CH4 consumption capacity than permanently flooded soils

The source says 'implying' and speaks of CH4 consumption CAPACITY. The 'so higher net emission' in the direction field is the extractor's inference. The very next sentence limits the claim: 'However, this is not always the case ... CH4 availability appears to play a more important role in regulating MOx than oxygen availability, which results in MOx sometimes being higher in wet soils than in dry soils' (refs 216-219). The source then adds that submerged phases favour anaerobic oxidation (AOM). The direction should be read as a tendency, not a rule.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Methanogen communities may take months to years to recover after re-wetting. This contrasts with the rapid reactivation seen in some floodplain sediments (see Boon 1997).

It cites ref 213, Juottonen 2012 AEM, on rewetted forestry-drained peatlands, not floodplains. The source gives recovery times 'ranging from days to years', not 'months to years'. Its examples are 3-6 days after summer inundation (ref 121, which is Boon, Mitchell & Lee 1997 Hydrobiologia 357:73-87 on ephemeral floodplain wetlands), more than 3 months in shrub bogs (ref 252), and 10-12 years in the rewetted peatlands (ref 213). So Cui itself cites Boon 1997 for the rapid recovery, which supports the contrast in the claim. confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Riverine flow-through wetland soils are mineral-rich (sediment dilution), with about one third of the organic C concentration of isolated depressional wetlands. Implied lower substrate density; CH4 not measured in this paper.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: implied: substrate per soil mass is lower in riverine floodplain soils than in depressional/permanent organic wetlands
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: The depressional wetland sites had higher (P < 0.001) organic content (146 ± 4.2 gC kg−1) and lower (P < 0.001) bulk density (0.55 ± 0.01 Mg m−3) than the riverine ones (50.1 ± 6.9 gC kg−1 and 0.74 ± 0.06 Mg m−3).
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote appears word for word in the Abstract (text conversion of the local PDF docs/refs/WFT/...Bernal...pdf, lines 21-22) and matches Table 2 (all depressional 146.4 ± 4.2 gC/kg total C; all riverine 50.1 ± 6.9). The Results say 'about three times', so 'about one third' is correct. Author and year agree with Crossref: issued 2012, online 2012-01-10; the local file name says 2011 because of the online-first date. CH4 was not measured; methane appears only in the Introduction. Four parts of the claim go beyond the source. (1) 'Sediment dilution' is the extractor's reading, not the authors' mechanism. The authors attribute the depressional-riverine gap to high forest productivity, shade that cools the site and slows litter decay, and recalcitrant woody litter. For the riverine site they note sediment and organic inputs from a 69 km² agricultural watershed. (2) The contrast is hydrogeomorphic (isolated depressional vs riverine flow-through), not permanent vs floodplain. Each site has one permanently flooded community and two intermittently flooded ones. The permanently flooded riverine Nelumbo floating bed has 86.6 gC/kg, only 1.5-2 times below the depressional sites. The riverine Phragmites marsh (26.6) and the mudflat (35.1) set the low mean. (3) The riverine site is a Lake Erie coastal, inland deltaic freshwater wetland with seiches (Old Woman Creek), not a classic seasonal river floodplain. (4) Per area (upper 30-35 cm, Table 3), the carbon pool is also lower: 4.18 ± 0.25 vs 1.50 ± 0.19 kgC/m², about 2.8 times. Soil bulk density in the Abstract is 0.55 vs 0.74 Mg/m³; Table 3 and the Results give 0.57 vs 0.77. There is only one site per type, both in Ohio. crossref.title: Comparing carbon sequestration in temperate freshwater wetland communities

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Tree stems are a CH4 pathway in temperate forested wetlands (up to 27% of seasonal ecosystem flux).
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: adds to per-area flux of forested (swamp/floodplain forest) wetlands; largest share in spring and winter
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: tree-mediated CH4 emissions contribute up to 27% of seasonal ecosystem CH4 flux in temperate forested wetland, with the largest relative contributions occurring in spring and winter.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote appears word for word in the Abstract on p. 2642 (checked with pdftotext on the local PDF docs/refs/WFT/Global Change Biology - 2015 - Pangala - ....pdf, line 26). The Crossref author and year match (Pangala, 2015). Caveats on scope from Table 1 and p. 2643: (1) 27% is the upper bound, reached only in spring, with young trees included and stem flux extrapolated to an assumed 10 m tree height. For mature trees alone the upper bound is 22.2% (spring, 10 m). On a 3 m stem basis the tree share is 6.4-16.8%. By season, including young trees: summer 8.8-13.5%, winter 16.8-24.6%, spring 16.8-26.6%. (2) This is a share of plot-scale ecosystem flux at a single site, Flitwick Moor, UK. The site is a spring-fed forested valley-mire peatland (fen and wet woodland), not a floodplain or river swamp, so labelling the direction 'swamp/floodplain forest' goes beyond the source. (3) Absolute tree flux is small: 1.42-13.2 g CH4 ha-1 day-1 per plot area, about 0.00014-0.0013 g CH4 m-2 day-1. crossref.title: The contribution of trees to ecosystem methane emissions in a temperate forested wetland

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Short-term flooding of a riparian grey alder forest made stems the dominant CH4 pathway (up to 88%), with a delayed CH4 response to flooding.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: flooded riparian forest: stems > soil surface; the lag lowers CH4 in short floods
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Contrary to N2O, the increase in CH4 fluxes delayed in response to flooding. [...] The stems contributed up to 88% of CH4 emissions to the stem-soil continuum during the investigated period
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The first author and year match Crossref (Schindler 2020, Sci. Rep. 10, 3204). I opened the full text as Europe PMC PMC7035275 XML, saved at scratchpad/perarea/schindler2020.txt. The quote appears word for word in the abstract, and the conclusions repeat the 88% line. Three things the claim does not say. (1) The flood was artificial: 55-70 m3 of water per day for two weeks, 8-21 Aug 2017. The site is Agali, Estonia (58°17'N), a hemiboreal grey alder stand on a former agricultural Gleysol, not a wetland. (2) The 88% is 'up to', the maximum across the pre, experimental and post periods on the flooded plot, after stem fluxes were upscaled to forest ground area (Fig. 6). The results say stem CH4 'dominated 7 times more'. In the abstract, stems are 'significantly higher than from soil after the flooding'. (3) All fluxes are in µg m-2 h-1, which is tiny. Soil CH4 went from -0.2 ± 1.7 (net uptake, before) to 12.8 ± 2.1 µg m-2 h-1 in the post period. Sustained for a whole year, 12.8 would be about 0.11 g CH4 m-2 yr-1. The paper says 'delayed' only once (abstract), plus 'Methane fluxes from the soil ... weighed in after the experiment'. It never says the lag lowers CH4 in short floods. confirmed_mechanisms.claim: A counter-case: in prairie pothole wetlands, permanently ponded wetlands were less responsive than temporary ones, attributed to higher sulfate. Permanent is not automatically higher where evapoconcentration raises sulfate.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: temporary more sensitive to temperature and depth; permanent suppressed by sulfate
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Methane emission rates from permanent wetlands were less sensitive to changes in temperature and water depth compared to temporary wetlands, likely due to higher sulfate concentrations in permanent wetlands.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Author (Bansal, Tangen, Finocchiaro) and year (online 2016-09-29, print Dec 2016) match Crossref. I found the quote word for word in the abstract of the full-text Springer HTML, accessed through an institutional subscription and saved as scratchpad/perarea/bansal2016_springer_clean.txt. Part of the claim is supported. (1) Permanent wetlands were less responsive: the Results give significantly steeper slopes for temporary wetlands, with significant group x temperature and group x depth interactions. The depth fits are ln(ug CH4 m-2 h-1) = 7.1 + 0.1*Depth(cm) for temporary wetlands and 5.9 + 0.03*Depth(cm) for permanent ones. (2) The sulfate explanation is hedged in the paper ('likely due to'). The Discussion also names water-column methanotrophy, because permanent wetlands hold water longer and in larger volumes. Sulfate is about 1002 mg/L in permanent wetlands versus 178 in temporary ones. (3) Permanent wetlands do not emit more per area in this study. The Results give overall means of 85.9 +/- 13.9 mg CH4 m-2 h-1 for temporary wetlands and 49.4 +/- 10.3 for permanent wetlands. The paper says the sulfate-dominated salinity comes from topography and groundwater interacting with sulfur- and carbonate-rich glacial till (Winter and Rosenberry 1998; Goldhaber et al. 2014). confirmed_mechanisms.first_author: Xu (Crossref record has given/family names swapped: 'Qin, Xu')

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: At a temperate fen, the largest CH4 fluxes coincided with late-summer water-table decline plus warming (drawdown degassing).
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: transient drawdown in warm season can give CH4 bursts
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Significant interannual differences, driven by high variability of large individual CH4 fluxes (ranging from 8.7 to 3833.1 mg CH4 m−2 d−1) occurring in the late summer, corresponded with a decline in water table level and an increase in air and peat temperature.

The core claim holds: at Sallie's Fen, New Hampshire (chamber CH4 measured weekly, 1 May to 31 Aug, 2000-2004), large individual late-summer fluxes of 8.7-3833.1 mg CH4 m-2 d-1 drove the interannual differences and coincided with a falling water table and rising air and peat temperature. confirmed_mechanisms.claim: LPJ-Bern treats tropical peatlands as inundated wetlands and gives inundated wetlands (south of 45N) a lower net CH4:CO2 conversion (2.40-4.15% of HR, including oxidation and tuning) than the production ratio for northern peatlands (20-25% in LPJ-WHyMe, before oxidation). confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Labile methanogen-available carbon (mainly plant litter) builds up during the dry season and is quickly used up after flooding, so floodplain flux peaks during rising water, before peak water. Flooding reaches fresh litter.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: early flood: floodplain flux per flooded area high (fresh substrate); later: declines as the pool depletes

This carbon pool is then rapidly depleted during the wet season. As a result, CH4 emission rates begin to decrease before the peak water phase.' The p. 2822 part of the claim is also in Sect. 2 (lead paragraph before 2.1): 'flooded areas expand at the onset of the wet season and engulf newly available plant litter; as a result, CH4 emissions from plant litter may peak before the height of the water table.' The paper also lists alternative explanations for the lag (macrophyte biomass, water-column oxidation, redox, pH) on p. 2826. (2) The model flux is per grid cell and driven by GRACE water height. The paper never states the direction 'per flooded area' or 'floodplain'. The claim's wording there is the extractor's interpretation.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Seasonally inundated systems should emit less per inundated area than continuously inundated wetlands, even in the wet season, because dry-season aerobic decomposition keeps the equilibrium soil carbon stock small; continuous anoxia builds a larger SOM stock that compensates slower anaerobic decomposition. confirmed_mechanisms.quote: In contrast, a tropical seasonally inundated system may experience extensive decomposition during the dry season but emit most of its CH4 during the wet season. Because the equilibrium carbon stock will be smaller, the CH4 fluxes will be smaller than the annual wetland even during the wet season.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote is verbatim on p. 1929 (Sect. 2.1.2); I checked it with pdftotext on the local PDF docs/refs/models/2011_Riley_CLM4Me_barriers.pdf, pages 5-6. Eq. (3), S = [beta(f - fbar) + fbar]/f with S <= 1, is on p. 1930. fbar is the annual-mean inundated fraction of the previous calendar year, weighted by heterotrophic respiration, and beta = 0.2 (Table 1). The value 0.95 is printed twice: in the Fig. B1 caption on p. 1947 ('CH4 flux-weighted, annual seasonal inundation factor ... The global average is 0.95') and in the Appendix B text on p. 1948 ('weighted by methane production ... the global average is 0.95'). Crossref gives Riley, 2011, which matches the claim. Four nuances. (1) The paper says anoxia 'partially' compensates. Compensation is complete only if decomposition is linear in pool size, the anaerobic rate is a fixed fraction of the aerobic rate, and the soil is in equilibrium. The claim's bare 'compensates' overstates this slightly. (2) The quote itself does not say 'per inundated area'. That basis comes from Eq. (2), where S multiplies production in the anaerobic or inundated part, and from Appendix B, Eq. (B4): 'all CH4 production comes from the instantaneously inundated fraction'. So the per-inundated-area reading is right. (3) The argument is theoretical: an idealized equilibrium soil-carbon model. It is not an observational result. CLM4Me itself uses gridcell-averaged heterotrophic respiration (RH) as a proxy for wetland production, and S corrects for that. (4) Useful for the theoretical range: Eq. (3) bounds the per-inundated-area production scaling between beta = 0.2 (fbar much smaller than f, a briefly flooded area) and 1 (fbar = f, permanently inundated). The production-weighted global mean of 0.95 shows the effect is small in aggregate but varies strongly between locations (Fig. B1).

crossref.title: Barriers to predicting changes in global terrestrial methane fluxes: analyses using CLM4Me, a methane biogeochemistry model integrated in CESM

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Floodplain trees vent CH4 from deep soil even when the water table is below the surface. The emitting area therefore extends beyond the flooded area: non-flooded riparian margins add 2.2-3.6 Tg yr-1 to 12.7-21.1 Tg yr-1 from inundated trees in the Amazon, and about 6.4 Tg yr-1 pantropically (17% of the flooded tropical tree flux).
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: floodplain emission per flooded area is underestimated if only inundated area emits
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: This raises the possibility that CH4 produced deep within the soil column can vent to the atmosphere via tree roots even when the water table (WT) is below the surface. If correct, this would challenge modelling efforts where inundation often defines the spatial extent of ecosystem CH4 production and emission.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: The quote appears word for word in the abstract (PMC8646147 full text). The numbers are printed as given in the abstract and in Sect. 3 ('From local to...'): 2.2–3.6 Tg CH4 yr-1 (the 95% CI around a best estimate of 2.8) comes from Amazon trees with WT < 0. It adds to 12.7–21.1 Tg CH4 yr-1 (95% CI around 16.4) from trees with WT at or above the surface (Table 2: F_sub 2.78 / F_sfc 16.35 / F_tot 19.14 for ctl, and 2.16–3.58 / 12.66–21.13 for the CI). The pantropical figure is 'approximately 6.4 Tg CH4 yr-1', which is 17% of a flooded tropical tree flux of about 37.1 Tg CH4 yr-1 (43.5 total, about 15% of total tree flux). Caveats: (1) All of these are JULES-modelled upscalings driven by a regression of stem flux on WT depth. They are tree-stem fluxes only, not whole-ecosystem floodplain emission, and no per-area g CH4 m-2 yr-1 value is given for either zone. (2) The 6.4 Tg covers all broadleaf tropical forests in the TRANSCOM tropical regions, which the abstract calls 'tropical wetland broad-leaf trees'. (3) The paper frames the result as extending the effective emitting area beyond flooded land (a larger emitting area). It does not say that the flux per flooded area is underestimated. The 'direction' field is the extractor's inference: the extra flux comes from non-inundated area, so the per-area flux on flooded land is unchanged. Only the per-unit-inundated-area emission would rise, and only if the riparian flux were attributed to the inundated area. (4) Crossref's issued date is 2021-12-06 (online) and the print date is 2022-01-24 (vol. 380, issue 2215). The citation year 2022 matches the print issue.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: LPJ-WSL (Hodson) scales CH4 per unit heterotrophic respiration with separate tropical and boreal factors, calibrated to the Amazon Central Basin (9.1 Tg CH4 yr-1) and the Hudson Bay Lowlands (2.3 Tg). The tropical factor is 7 times the boreal one (D: 0.175/0.025).
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: tropical inundated wetland > boreal wetland (per unit Rh, x7)
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: To account for broad ecosystem differences in CH4 emitting capacity between tropical and boreal wetlands, we scaled Rh and S through a combination of two latitudinal scaling factors (FT and FB) and surface temperature. ... resulting in FT = 0.175 and FB = 0.025
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed. The quote is verbatim in para [8] (p.1 right column to p.2 left column of the local PDF, docs/refs/models/2011_Hodson_ENSO_wetland_ch4_iav.pdf). The model is E(x,t) = F(x)·b·Rh(x,t)·S(x,t), with b = 0.03 mol CH4 per mol C respired (para [5]). FT and FB were fitted to the Hudson Bay Lowlands (2.3 Tg CH4 yr-1, Pickett-Heaps et al. 2010) and the Amazon Central Basin (9.1 Tg CH4 yr-1, Melack et al. 2004), which gives FT = 0.175 and FB = 0.025. FT/FB = 7 is arithmetically right. Four caveats. (1) The factor multiplies Rh×S, where S is the inundated wetland fraction, so it is per unit Rh per unit inundated area. It is not a per-area flux ratio, and the tropical-to-boreal flux ratio also depends on Rh, which is itself higher in the tropics. (2) The factor applied in each grid cell is a temperature-weighted blend, F(x) = s(x)·FT + (1 − s(x))·FB, with s = exp(T(x) − Tmax)/[divisor lost in the PDF text extraction], Tmax = 303.35 K and T the 1960–1990 mean. So the x7 holds only at the pure tropical and pure boreal ends. (3) The paper never uses the name 'LPJ-WSL'; it says only that Rh comes from the LPJ DGVM (the authors are at WSL). (4) The paper does not separate 'inundated' wetland from 'boreal wetland' as classes. The tropical/boreal split is by latitude and temperature, and S is satellite-derived inundated area everywhere (Prigent et al. 2007). For the boreal regions S is the mean monthly Prigent inundation. Rice regions are excluded. The resulting mean global emission is 171.2 Tg CH4 yr-1 over 1950–2005.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: WetCHARTs computes per-area flux as a global scale factor times heterotrophic respiration times a temperature term. Floodplain and peatland per-area fluxes differ only through Rh and temperature; there is no type-specific factor.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: per-area difference set only by Rh and T
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: F (t, x) = s A (t, x) R (t, x) q10^(T(t,x)/10), where A(t, x) is the wetland extent fraction, R(t, x) is the C heterotrophic respiration per unit area at time t
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Confirmed from the text conversion of the local PDF (docs/refs/models/2017_Bloom_WetCHARTs_v1.pdf, scratchpad perarea/2017_Bloom_WetCHARTs_v1.txt lines 126-146). Sect. 2.1 prints Eq. (1) F(t,x) = s A(t,x) R(t,x) q10^(T(t,x)/10), with F in mg CH4 m-2 day-1, A the wetland extent fraction, R the C heterotrophic respiration per unit area, q10^(T/10) the temperature dependence of the CH4:C respired ratio (T is surface skin temperature), and s a global scaling factor. The quote matches. Location fix: Eq. (1) is on p. 2143, not p. 2142 (the p. 2143 running header comes before Sect. 2.1). Two points for the basis. (1) F is per grid-cell area because A multiplies it; the flux per wetland area is F/A = s R q10^(T/10). (2) s is set per ensemble member (s_c, Eq. 3) so the global total is 124.5, 166 or 207.5 Tg CH4 yr-1 (Table 1), and R comes from 8 MsTMIP models plus CARDAMOM at grid-cell level, not from wetland-specific carbon. Sect. 4.1 (p. 2149) names this as an error source: the wetland and non-inundated areas in a cell differ in carbon uptake and dead organic matter. The paper has no term for wetland type anywhere. The words peat, floodplain and bog do not appear in the body text, so 'no type-specific factor' is correct. Type contrasts can come only through R and T (plus the extent term A, which sets area and not the flux per wetland area).

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: Tropical wetland water tables swing more than northern ones: standing water in the wet season, often below 1 m in the dry season. The production base rate R0 is mainly a function of mean temperature.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: tropical seasonal wetlands: high wet-season rates, near-zero dry season
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: In the tropics, there is usually standing water during the wet season and very low (often below 1 m soil depth) water levels during the dry season. The amplitude of seasonal variations in the water table is, in general, larger in tropical wetlands.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Checked against the local PDF docs/refs/models/2001_Walter_modern_wetland_ch4_part1.pdf (pdftotext -raw). Author and year match Crossref (Walter, Heimann, Matthews 2001, JGR 106(D24) 34189-34206). (1) The quote is printed word for word in Sect. 6 Summary and Conclusion, p. 34204: 'In the tropics, there is usually standing water during the wet season and very low (often below 1 m soil depth) water levels during the dry season. The amplitude of seasonal variations in the water table is, in general, larger in tropical wetlands.' Sect. 4.2.3, p. 34197 says the same about Fig. 5 (Panama). Caveat on basis: the sentence comes right after 'Simulated water levels in HNH wetlands are highest during the winter...', so it describes the paper's MODELLED water tables, not observations. (2) The R0 claim holds, but its location is wrong. It is Eq. (2) in Sect. 2 (Methane Model), p. 34191, not Sect. 3.1: R0(x,y) = 0.45 + 0.1*T_mean - 0.001*NPP_tot, 'which shows that R0(x,y) is mainly dependent upon T_mean(x,y)'. T_mean is the mean annual temperature, and NPP also enters the regression (Sect. 5.2 says R0 is 'a function of NPP and the mean annual temperature'). R0 was fitted to six test sites, and Sect. 6 says R0 'is too large'. (3) The 'near-zero dry season' direction comes from a model assumption, not a measured flux. Sect. 3.1, p. 34191 says 'in tropical wetlands, soils dry for a certain period of time; that is, in the model there is no wetland during the dry season (Figure 5, Panama)', and Sect. 4.2.3, p. 34197 says 'most methane emissions take place in the wet season'. The paper gives no per-area wet-season rate in these passages, so 'high wet-season rates' is not quantified here. No per-area flux numbers are claimed or checked.

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: In a reduced process model calibrated on mid-latitude wetlands, emissions peak when the water table is at or just above the soil surface. Oxidation is a significant sink in some systems.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: shallow flooding/saturation maximizes flux; deep flooding or drawdown lowers it
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Peak fluxes consistently occur when the water table is at or just above the soil surface and are strongly modulated by wetland-specific parameters, with oxidation acting as a significant sink in some systems.
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Crossref agrees on the author (McNicol, Layton, Basu), the year (2026) and the journal (Biogeosciences 23(7), 2309-2333, published 9 Apr 2026). The quoted sentence appears word for word in the abstract on p. 2309 (Crossref abstract and local text conversion of docs/refs/models/2026_McNicol_reduced_process_wetland_ch4.pdf). 'Calibrated on mid-latitude wetlands' is also confirmed. Sect. 3 says the model parameters are calibrated with observations from six small depressional Prairie Pothole wetlands at Cottonwood Lake, North Dakota: three permanent (P1, P3, P8) and three temporary (T5, T6, T9). Each wetland was fitted separately with a genetic-algorithm nRMSE minimisation, and D was fixed at 1.3 cm2 d-1. These are prairie marsh ponds, not peatlands. The direction is supported by Sect. 5.1, which says emissions are 'typically suppressed under both drought and deep inundation'. Two caveats apply. (1) The peak is not always just above the surface. The paper cites Calabrese et al. (2021) for a critical depth of about 50 cm above the surface, and says the peak moves further above the surface as temperature rises. (2) When the production-decay parameter p1 = 0, emissions reach a plateau with increasing inundation rather than falling. So 'deep flooding lowers flux' depends on the parameters. It holds when production declines with water depth (substrate dilution, p1 > 0) or when oxidation stays active. The paper also reports that oxidation is a larger fraction of production in temporary wetlands than in permanent ones (Fig. 6). The paper gives no per-area annual flux values, so no rows were checked.

crossref.title: Understanding the balance between methane production and oxidation from wetlands: insights from a reduced process-based model

confirmed_mechanisms.claim: WETCHIMP-generation global models lack an explicit treatment of floodplains, and of lateral water transport within and between grid cells.
confirmed_mechanisms.direction: model gap: floodplain vs peatland differences not represented
confirmed_mechanisms.quote: Such features include (i) lateral transport of water and groundwater dynamics within ... and between grid cells, and explicit treatments of floodplains and mangroves
confirmed_mechanisms.check_note: Quote is verbatim, Sect. 5 'Summary and conclusions', p. 637 (the ellipsis drops '(beyond the assumptions of the TOPMODEL formulation)'). Exact wording: features 'still missing, or are crudely represented, in almost all of the models ... include (i) lateral transport of water and groundwater dynamics within ... and between grid cells, and explicit treatments of floodplains and mangroves'. Caveats: (1) the source says 'missing or crudely represented in almost all', not that all WETCHIMP models lack them; (2) the extractor's 'direction' label ('floodplain vs peatland differences not represented') is NOT in the source. The paper names no per-area flux difference between floodplains and peatlands and gives no g CH4 m-2 yr-1 values for either class here. It supports only the qualitative model-gap statement. Author/year match Crossref.
